About this edition

This is the second edition of the MYP 1 mathematics coursebook. It was rebuilt from the first-edition MYP Mathematics 1 Student Coursebook, which remains the principal content reference and is preserved unchanged in the project archive.

The edition keeps the first edition's chapter scope and its visual identity, and rebuilds the teaching sequence around inquiry: engagement, inquiry questions, investigation, observation, mathematical conclusion, formal development, worked examples, extensive visual practice, and application, assessment and reflection.

All classroom data sets are simulated and are labelled as such. Real data would require provenance, so no claim in this book rests on unverified statistics.

No publisher, ISBN, print specification or commercial print-readiness claim is made in this file. The book is produced as an A4 review copy: fonts are embedded, pagination is continuous and every page has been checked for overflow.

How to use this book

Each chapter follows the same sequence, so you always know what is coming next. The sequence is deliberate: you investigate before you are told the rule, because a rule you have discovered is a rule you can defend.

The chapter sequence

  1. Engagement. A short situation that raises the question the chapter will answer.
  2. Inquiry questions. Factual, conceptual and debatable questions that frame the chapter.
  3. Investigation. A task you complete before the formal teaching: record evidence in a table and look for a pattern.
  4. Observation and discovery. What you noticed, stated in your own words and compared with a partner.
  5. Mathematical conclusion. The rule that the evidence supports, written as a general statement.
  6. Formal development. The explanation, definitions and notation, with the reasoning made explicit.
  7. Worked examples. Problem, visual representation, mathematical reasoning, step-by-step solution, final answer and interpretation.
  8. Practice. Separated into Criterion A, B, C and D practice, with visual representations throughout.
  9. Application, assessment and reflection. Real-context tasks, criterion-based assessment practice and a review of your progress.

How to use this book

The four MYP mathematics criteria

A · Knowing and understanding

Apply knowledge to familiar and unfamiliar problems, and check results.

B · Investigating patterns

Investigate, describe patterns, generalise and justify — recognising, describing and verifying patterns at Year 1 level rather than producing formal proofs.

C · Communicating

Use correct mathematical language, notation and representations, and reason coherently.

D · Applying mathematics in real-life contexts

Apply mathematics to authentic situations, identify relevant information and comment on the accuracy and sense of the result.

Working with this book

  • Practice is separated by criterion so that you can see which skill a task is training. Criterion B practice is additional genuine pattern investigation, not a repeat of the teaching.
  • Visuals are part of the mathematics. Where a task supplies a diagram, grid, table, number line or model, use it; where it asks you to sketch, your drawing is part of the answer.
  • Answers and student-facing reasoning are collected at the back of the book, with formula bank, glossary and references.
  • Every chapter ends with project connections: a Service as Action opportunity, a Community Project connection and a Personal Project connection for MYP 5.
MYP Mathematics 1 · Student coursebookIntroduction
MYP 1 · Student coursebook

MYP mathematics and this coursebook

The IB Middle Years Programme asks students to inquire into concepts through global contexts, to develop approaches to learning (ATL) skills, and to act on what they learn through service as action. In mathematics this means more than practising procedures: students investigate patterns, justify generalisations, communicate with precise language and apply mathematics to situations that matter to them.

MYP mathematics is organised into four branches — number, algebra, geometry and trigonometry, and statistics and probability — and the programme recommends at least 50 hours of teaching per subject each year. This coursebook covers the Year 1 content of those branches across ten chapters, grouped into five parts.

Assessment in MYP mathematics uses four equally weighted criteria, each with a maximum of 8: A knowing and understanding, B investigating patterns, C communicating, and D applying mathematics in real-life contexts. This book trains each criterion explicitly, and says so on the page where the training happens.

MYP mathematics and this coursebook

Projects, service and action

Service as Action

Each chapter includes a service opportunity with a community need, a mathematical connection, a proposed action, an expected impact and a student reflection. Completing an exercise is not service: service requires action that benefits others and reflection on that action.

Community Project

MYP students completing the programme in Year 3 or Year 4 complete a community project. Each chapter offers a student-led project idea with a research question, the mathematics involved, an action or outcome, beneficiaries and evidence. Follow your school's requirements and supervision.

Personal Project (MYP 5)

Students completing MYP in Year 5 complete a personal project. Each chapter offers an adaptable MYP 5-oriented extension with a personal interest, a learning goal, a product, the mathematics involved, a process and evidence. It is deliberately different from the community project and from service as action.

What this book does not claim

  • Programme requirements quoted here follow the official IB MYP curriculum, mathematics and projects pages and the MYP general regulations. Everything else — the chapter sequence, the investigations, the practice sets and the project ideas — is author-designed material built to serve those requirements, and is not an IB publication.
  • No ISBN, publisher, imprint or print specification is claimed. The file is an A4 review copy with embedded fonts and continuous pagination, produced for proofing and classroom review rather than for commercial print production.

Part I · The grammar of number · MYP Year 1 · Chapter 01

Number systems and place value

Numbers are read through their places, and every number belongs to a family. This chapter builds the number sense the rest of the book relies on: place value, equivalent representations, comparison, rounding and sensible accuracy.

Inquiry questions
  • Factual: Which number families does a number such as −3, 0 or 0.25 belong to, and what makes each family different?
  • Conceptual: Why does the position of a digit change its value, and why can a zero be important even when it adds nothing?
  • Debatable: When is a rounded figure honest, and when does it hide something a reader needs to know?
Second edition
Part I · The grammar of number
01

Number systems and place value

Ten digits are enough to write any number we can name. Their power comes from position: the same symbol can mean seven, seventy or seven thousandths.

Engage

A museum label says “about 49,000 objects”, while an inventory says “48,672 objects”. Which number would you put on a poster? Which would you use to check the collection? What changes when we round?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Form
Related concepts: Quantity, Representation
Global context: Orientation in space and time

Statement of inquiry: The position of a digit in a base-ten system encodes its value, so a small set of symbols can represent any magnitude when place and zero are used consistently.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What is the value of a digit in a given position?
  • Conceptual: Why is zero essential, and how can one number have several equivalent representations?
  • Debatable: When is “about 2,000” more useful than the exact count?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to evaluate and improve a mathematical claim, students must test the claim on several cases, find a counterexample if one exists, and revise the statement so it is accurate.
Getting ready

Learning intentions and prerequisite check

You are learning to

  • Understand how natural numbers, whole numbers, integers and rational numbers are related.
  • Know that the value of a digit depends on its place in a base-ten number.
  • Write whole numbers and decimals in expanded form and return to standard form.
  • Compare and order integers and decimals using place value and a number line.
  • Round to a stated place and choose a reasonable level of accuracy in context.
  • Estimate a result and explain whether the estimate is likely to be too high or too low.

Success criteria

  • I can classify a number and explain the role of zero.
  • I can state the value of any digit in a whole number or decimal.
  • I can move between standard form, expanded form and a number line.
  • I can order positive and negative numbers and justify the order.
  • I can round to a stated place and avoid an over-precise answer.
  • I can estimate, check exactly, and explain the difference.

Ready check

Try these without a calculator. They check the ideas this chapter builds on.

  1. 1.R1Write “four thousand and sixty” using digits.Ready
  2. 1.R2Which is greater, 0.5 or 0.45? Explain using hundredths.Ready
  3. 1.R3Calculate 8 × 7.Ready
  4. 1.R4What is 100 more than 2,950?Ready
  5. 1.R5Write 7/10 as a decimal.Ready
  6. 1.R6Put −2, 0, 3 and −5 in order from least to greatest.Ready
How to use this chapter

Work through the examples before the practice. Use the diagrams to explain your thinking. Answers and student-facing reasoning are at the back of this proof. If more than two ready-check items are incorrect, review place value to hundreds and simple fractions before continuing.

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 1 · Number systems and place value
Chapter 1 · Investigation · before 1.1

Investigate · Which numbers belong together?

Your task

Sort these numbers into the families below. A number can belong to more than one family, so tick every column that applies: 7, −3, 0, 3/4, 0.25.

NumberNaturalWholeIntegerRational
7
−3
0
3/4
0.25

What do you notice?

  • Which number belongs to every family except the natural numbers, and what does that tell you about zero?
  • Which family contains all of the others, and how can you see that on a number line?
Observation. Natural numbers count from 1. Whole numbers add 0. Integers add the negatives. Rational numbers include every fraction and every terminating or repeating decimal, so 3/4 and 0.25 are both rational.
Mathematical conclusion

Each family sits inside the next one, and a number line gives every number a position. Values increase from left to right and 0 is the boundary between negative and positive.

Chapter 1 · 1.1 · Number systems and the number line

Counting numbers, zero and negatives

Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1,2,3,…1,2,3,\ldots1,2,3,…. In this book, whole numbers are the natural numbers together with zero: 0,1,2,3,…0,1,2,3,\ldots0,1,2,3,…. Integers include the whole numbers and their negatives: …,−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3,…\ldots,-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3,\ldots…,−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3,….

A number line gives every number a position. Values increase from left to right. Zero is the boundary between negative and positive numbers; it is neither positive nor negative.

Worked example 1

Classify −4-4−4, 000 and 121212.

  1. −4-4−4 is an integer and a rational number, but not whole or natural.
  2. 000 is whole, an integer and rational, but not natural in this book.
  3. 121212 is natural, whole, an integer and rational.

Each number can belong to more than one family.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Chapter 1 · 1.1 · Number systems and the number line

Rational numbers and number families

A rational number can be written as a fraction ab\frac{a}{b}ba​ where aaa and bbb are integers and b≠0b\neq 0b=0. Terminating decimals such as 1.21.21.2 and fractions such as 58\frac{5}{8}85​ are rational. Every integer is rational because, for example, −4=−41-4=\frac{-4}{1}−4=1−4​.

Misconception check

“Zero is not a number because it means nothing.” Zero is a number with a precise position. It also holds a place: 305305305 is not the same as 353535.

Worked example 2

Order −7,−2,0,3,5-7,-2,0,3,5−7,−2,0,3,5 from least to greatest.

  1. On a number line, more negative values lie further left.
  2. Read from left to right: −7,−2,0,3,5-7,-2,0,3,5−7,−2,0,3,5.

Coldest to warmest: −7 ∘C,−2 ∘C,0 ∘C,3 ∘C,5 ∘C-7\,^\circ\text{C},-2\,^\circ\text{C},0\,^\circ\text{C},3\,^\circ\text{C},5\,^\circ\text{C}−7∘C,−2∘C,0∘C,3∘C,5∘C.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 1 · Number systems and place value
Chapter 1 · Investigation · before 1.2

Investigate · What does a zero do?

Your task

For each pair, state the value of the highlighted zero and describe the job it is doing.

PairValue of the zeroJob it is doing
305 and 35
0.4 and 0.40
4.05 and 4.5
40 and 400
0.305 and 0.35

What do you notice?

  • In which pairs does the zero change the value, and in which does it not?
  • What single rule explains the difference between the two kinds of zero?
Observation. A zero can hold a place (in 305 it holds the tens place) or mark an empty position. Adding a zero to the right of a whole number multiplies it by 10; adding a zero after the last decimal digit leaves the value unchanged, because 0.4 = 0.40.
Mathematical conclusion

Position gives a digit its value, so a zero is never simply “nothing”: it is an instruction about place.

Chapter 1 · 1.2 · Place value and the role of zero

Position gives a digit its value

In a base-ten system, each position is worth ten times the position to its right. The decimal point separates whole-number places from fractional places. A zero can be a placeholder: it keeps the other digits in the correct positions.

Worked example 3

State the value of the 4 in 3,048.3073{,}048.3073,048.307 and calculate 36.2×1036.2\times 1036.2×10.

  1. The 4 is in the tens place, so its value is 404040.
  2. Multiplying by 10 shifts every digit one place left: 36.2×10=36236.2\times 10=36236.2×10=362.

The decimal point does not “move” by itself; the digits shift relative to it.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Practice 1.2 · Place value and zero

  1. 1.2.1State the value of the underlined digit. (a) 6,742 (b) 23.58 (c) 8,106 (d) 0.204Fluency
  2. 1.2.2Write the number represented by 4,000 + 600 + 30 + 2.Fluency
  3. 1.2.3Calculate. (a) 36.2 × 10 (b) 5.48 × 100 (c) 920 ÷ 10 (d) 7.3 ÷ 100Fluency
  4. 1.2.4In 2.06, what does the zero do? What number results if the zero is removed, and how much larger is it?Reasoning
Chapter 1 · 1.2 · Place value and the role of zero

Zero, decimals and digit cards

Adding a zero to the right of a whole number multiplies it by 10, but adding a zero after a decimal may leave the value unchanged: 0.4=0.400.4=0.400.4=0.40. Multiplying or dividing by powers of ten shifts digits, not just the decimal point.

Worked example 4

Use 5, 0, 8 and 2 once each to make the greatest and least four-digit numbers.

  1. Greatest: put the largest digits in the highest places: 8,5208{,}5208,520.
  2. Least: the first digit cannot be 0, so start with 2, then use the smallest remaining digits: 2,0582{,}0582,058.

Greatest 8,5208{,}5208,520; least 2,0582{,}0582,058.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Practice 1.2 · Place value and zero

  1. 1.2.5Which is larger, 3.5 or 3.05? Explain using place value, not the number of digits.Reasoning
  2. 1.2.6A warehouse receives 24 boxes with 100 pencils in each box. Write the total and state the value of the digit 2 in your answer.Application
  3. 1.2.7Test the claim “adding a zero to the right of a number multiplies it by 10” on 4, 0.4 and 4.50. Then write a corrected rule.Reasoning
  4. 1.2.8Using 5, 0, 8 and 2 exactly once each, make the greatest and least four-digit numbers. Explain why the least cannot begin with 0.Challenge
Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 1 · Number systems and place value
Chapter 1 · Investigation · before 1.3

Investigate · One number, many forms

Your task

Write 4,506.07 in expanded form and in words. Then rebuild a number from its parts: 3×100 + 0×10 + 7×1 + 5×0.1 + 2×0.01.

FormExample
Standard form4,506.07
Expanded form
Word form
From parts3×100 + 0×10 + 7×1 + 5×0.1 + 2×0.01 =

What do you notice?

  • Which form makes the value of each digit easiest to see?
  • Why does the 0×10 term matter even though it adds nothing?
Observation. Expanded form writes a number as the sum of the values of its digits. The zero terms show which places are empty, so nothing is lost when the number is rebuilt: 3×100 + 0×10 + 7×1 + 5×0.1 + 2×0.01 = 307.52.
Mathematical conclusion

Equivalent representations have the same value but make different features visible. Choose the form that shows the feature you need.

Chapter 1 · 1.3 · Expanded form and equivalent representations

One number, several useful forms

Expanded form writes a number as the sum of the values of its digits. It makes the contribution of each place visible. Standard form is the usual compact way of writing the number.

Worked example 5

Write 30.7830.7830.78 in expanded form, then return to standard form.

  1. Identify each place: 3 tens, 0 ones, 7 tenths, 8 hundredths.
  2. Expanded form: 30+0.7+0.0830+0.7+0.0830+0.7+0.08.
  3. Adding the parts gives 30.7830.7830.78 again.

30.78=30+0.7+0.08=3×10+7×0.1+8×0.0130.78=30+0.7+0.08=3\times10+7\times0.1+8\times0.0130.78=30+0.7+0.08=3×10+7×0.1+8×0.01.

Why zero still matters

407.3=400+7+0.3407.3=400+7+0.3407.3=400+7+0.3. The zero tens do not add value, but they keep the 4 in the hundreds place and the 7 in the ones place.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Practice 1.3 · Expanded form

  2. 1.3.2Write as a standard number. (a) 4 × 100 + 9 × 10 + 6 × 1 (b) 6 × 1 + 5 × 0.1 + 8 × 0.01 (c) 2 × 1,000 + 7 × 10 + 3 × 0.001Fluency

Chapter 1 · 1.3 · Expanded form and equivalent representations

Explain the structure, not just the answer

Equivalent representations have the same value but can make different features visible. A place-value chart shows positions; expanded form shows contributions; a number line shows order and distance.

Worked example 6

Explain why 2×0.1+5×0.012\times0.1+5\times0.012×0.1+5×0.01 is ten times 2×0.01+5×0.0012\times0.01+5\times0.0012×0.01+5×0.001.

  1. First expression: 0.2+0.05=0.250.2+0.05=0.250.2+0.05=0.25.
  2. Second expression: 0.02+0.005=0.0250.02+0.005=0.0250.02+0.005=0.025.
  3. Each digit has moved one place to the left, so each contribution is ten times as large.

0.25=10×0.0250.25=10\times0.0250.25=10×0.025.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Communicate

When you explain a representation, name the place, state its value, and say what the representation makes easy to see.

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 1 · Number systems and place value
Chapter 1 · Investigation · before 1.4

Investigate · Compare, then round

Your task

Compare each pair, then round the first number to the place stated.

PairLarger valueRounded value
0.7 and 0.07
2.35 and 2.4
−3 and −5
3.47 to the nearest tenth
0.995 to two decimal places

What do you notice?

  • What do you compare first when the whole parts are equal?
  • Why does 0.995 round to 1.00 rather than to 0.99?
Observation. Align the decimal points and compare from the highest place downwards. For negative numbers the order reverses. Rounding looks at the digit immediately to the right of the target place, and a carry can travel left through a run of 9s.
Mathematical conclusion

A rounded number is a statement about a range, not an exact value, so always state the place or unit you used.

Chapter 1 · 1.4 · Comparing, ordering and rounding

Compare place by place

To compare decimals, align the decimal points and compare digits from the highest place downwards. Add trailing zeros if helpful: 0.5=0.500.5=0.500.5=0.50. For negative numbers, the number further left on the number line is smaller.

Worked example 7

Order 0.7,0.07,0.77,0.7070.7,0.07,0.77,0.7070.7,0.07,0.77,0.707 from least to greatest.

  1. Write with three decimal places: 0.700,0.070,0.770,0.7070.700,0.070,0.770,0.7070.700,0.070,0.770,0.707.
  2. Compare: 0.070<0.700<0.707<0.7700.070<0.700<0.707<0.7700.070<0.700<0.707<0.770.

0.07,0.7,0.707,0.770.07,0.7,0.707,0.770.07,0.7,0.707,0.77.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Practice 1.4 · Compare, order and round

  1. 1.4.1Insert <, > or =. (a) 0.5 0.50 (b) 2.7 2.68 (c) −3 −5Fluency
  2. 1.4.2Order from least to greatest: 0.7, 0.07, 0.77, 0.707.Fluency
Misconception check

“More digits means a larger decimal.” Not always: 6.09<6.16.09<6.16.09<6.1 because 6.1=6.106.1=6.106.1=6.10.

Chapter 1 · 1.4 · Comparing, ordering and rounding

Round to a stated place

To round, identify the target place and look at the digit immediately to its right. If that digit is 5 or more, round up; otherwise round down. This book uses the usual convention that a 5 in the deciding place rounds up.

Worked example 8

Round 59.9659.9659.96 to the nearest tenth.

  1. The target is the tenths place: 9. The deciding digit is 6.
  2. Round 9 tenths up to 10 tenths, which is one whole.
  3. The result is 60.060.060.0. The trailing zero records tenths.

59.96≈60.059.96\approx60.059.96≈60.0 to the nearest tenth.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Practice 1.4 · Compare, order and round

  1. 1.4.3Round 8,647 to the nearest (a) hundred (b) ten.Fluency
  2. 1.4.4Round 3.746 to the nearest hundredth and 0.897 to the nearest tenth.Fluency
  3. 1.4.5Round 59.96 to the nearest tenth. Explain why the whole-number part changes.Reasoning
Chapter 1 · 1.4 · Comparing, ordering and rounding

Rounding in context

A rounded number is not the exact value; it is a statement about a range. Always state the place or unit used. In accountability contexts, give the exact figure as well as any rounded headline.

Worked example 9

Give three decimals that round to 6.5 to the nearest tenth, then describe all possible values.

  1. Examples: 6.45,6.50,6.5496.45,6.50,6.5496.45,6.50,6.549.
  2. The lower boundary is 6.45 because the deciding digit is 5.
  3. The upper boundary is just below 6.55, because 6.55 would round to 6.6.

All values from 6.45 inclusive up to but not including 6.55.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 1 · Number systems and place value
Chapter 1 · Investigation · before 1.5

Investigate · Estimate first, then check

Your task

Estimate each calculation using friendly numbers, then calculate exactly and find the difference.

CalculationEstimateExactDifference
48 × 31
5.9 + 7.2
3.87 × 4.1
198 ÷ 9.8

What do you notice?

  • Which estimates were close enough to catch a mistake?
  • What happens to the error when you round one number up and the other down?
Observation. An estimate uses friendly numbers to predict a result. Rounding one factor up and another down can cancel the errors, so the estimate can be closer than either rounding alone: 48 × 31 ≈ 50 × 30 = 1,500 and the exact value is 1,488.
Mathematical conclusion

Estimate first, then check: the estimate tells you whether the exact answer is reasonable before you trust it.

Chapter 1 · 1.5 · Estimation and sensible accuracy

Estimate first, then check

An estimate uses friendly numbers to predict a result or check whether an exact answer is reasonable. State the rounding you used. When one number is rounded up and another down, the estimate may be high or low; an exact check tells you which.

Worked example 10

Estimate 58×3158\times3158×31, then calculate exactly.

  1. Round to the nearest ten: 60×30=1,80060\times30=1{,}80060×30=1,800.
  2. Exactly: 58×31=1,79858\times31=1{,}79858×31=1,798.
  3. The estimate is 2 high.

Estimate 1,800; exact 1,798.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Reasoning habit

Ask: “What is this estimate for?” A quick headline, a budget check and an inventory may need different accuracy.

Chapter 1 · 1.5 · Estimation and sensible accuracy

Choose accuracy for a purpose

Extra digits are not automatically more truthful. A calculation can produce many decimal places even when the original measurement was only accurate to the nearest centimetre. Report a level of accuracy that the context can support.

Worked example 11

A library has 1,247,936 books. Suggest a figure for a short public notice.

  1. A headline does not need the exact count.
  2. “About 1,250,000 books” to the nearest ten thousand is readable.
  3. An inventory or audit should use 1,247,936 exactly.

Match the accuracy to the purpose, and state the rounding used.

Common slips

  • Forgetting a placeholder zero: 305 is not 35.
  • Comparing decimals by counting digits.
  • Rounding 39.95 to 39.9 instead of 40.0.
  • Assuming an estimate must be high or low without checking.

Explain how you know

  • Name the place before stating a digit’s value.
  • Use a number line to justify an order.
  • State the target place before rounding.
  • Compare an estimate with an exact result when possible.

Chapter review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • Number families are nested: natural ⊂\subset⊂ whole ⊂\subset⊂ integer ⊂\subset⊂ rational.
  • Place value gives each digit a value; zero can hold a place.
  • Expanded form shows each digit’s contribution.
  • Compare decimals place by place, not by counting digits.
  • Rounding records a range and a chosen accuracy.
  • Estimates are useful when checked and matched to purpose.

Vocabulary

natural number · whole number · integer · rational number · place value · placeholder · decimal point · expanded form · standard form · number line · rounding · estimate · accuracy

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 1 · Number systems and place value
Chapter 1 · Action and projects

Project connections

Mathematics becomes service and action when it answers a need that other people have. Each connection below is student-led: choose one, plan it with your teacher and follow your school’s requirements and supervision.

Service as Action

Community need
Learners in a feeder primary school hesitate when reading large numbers and decimals aloud.
Mathematical connection
Place value, the role of zero, expanded form and rounding (sections 1.1–1.5).
Proposed action
Plan and run a 30-minute “reading numbers” session using place-value cards and a noticeboard sorting task; keep a log of the misconceptions you meet.
Expected impact
Younger learners can read a number with its places named and can question a rounded figure.
Student reflection
Record which explanation worked, how you checked understanding, and what you would change next time.

Community Project connection

Project idea
A “numbers you can trust” audit of public notices around the school and local market.
Community need
Public notices often round without saying so, so readers cannot judge the size of the error.
Research question
How often do local notices give the exact figure alongside a rounded one, and when does the rounding mislead?
Mathematics
Place value, rounding ranges and estimation.
Action and outcome
Collect 20 notices, classify each as exact or rounded, and produce a one-page guide for the school office.
Beneficiaries
School office staff, families and local shopkeepers.
Evidence
Notice log, classified data set, final guide, photographs of the notices.

Personal Project connection · MYP 5

Personal interest
Data journalism and how reported figures are chosen.
Learning goal
To apply rounding and estimation critically to real reports.
Product or outcome
A short article or poster that checks whether three reported figures are stated to a sensible accuracy.
Mathematics
Place value, rounding ranges, estimation and percentage error.
Process
Collect reports, classify each figure, recompute the range it implies, and evaluate the claim.
Evidence
Product, process journal and an evaluation against the stated learning goal. This is an MYP 5-oriented extension: follow your school's Personal Project requirements and supervision.

Service as Action is not the same as completing an exercise: it requires action that benefits others and a reflection on that action. The Community Project connection suits the MYP community project completed by students finishing MYP in Year 3 or Year 4, and the Personal Project connection is an adaptable MYP 5-oriented extension. They are deliberately different from one another.

Part I · The grammar of number · MYP Year 1 · Chapter 02

Powers, expanded form and order of operations

Powers are a compact way to record repeated multiplication, and they explain why place value, square and cube roots, and the order of operations all behave the way they do.

Inquiry questions
  • Factual: What does an exponent record, and what do 7^1 and 7^0 mean?
  • Conceptual: Why does place value work as a system of powers of ten, and why do squares, cubes and roots reverse each other?
  • Debatable: When does a mathematical model such as “each fold doubles the thickness” stop describing a real object?
Second edition
Part I · The grammar of number
02

Powers, expanded form and order of operations

A power is a compressed instruction: it records how many copies of a factor to multiply. A shared order of operations keeps that compression unambiguous.

Engage

A storage label says “10 TB”. A computer reports the same space as “about 9.09 TiB”. Has storage disappeared? And when someone writes 2+3×42+3\times42+3×4, what must we agree before the expression has one meaning?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Form
Related concepts: Simplification, Quantity
Global context: Scientific and technical innovation

Statement of inquiry: Compressing repeated multiplication into a power, and agreeing on the order in which operations apply, allows complex calculations to be recorded compactly and reproduced reliably.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What does 535^353 mean? Which operation comes first in 6+2×36+2\times36+2×3?
  • Conceptual: Why does an exponent of 1 leave the base unchanged? How can 2102^{10}210 and 10310^3103 be compared fairly?
  • Debatable: Should a calculator decide the meaning of an expression, or should the writer make the meaning visible?
ATL · Transfer. In order for a student to transfer a rule to a new situation, students must check whether the structure is the same, apply the rule carefully, and test the result with an example or counterexample.
Getting ready

Learning intentions and prerequisite check

You are learning to

  • Understand a power as repeated multiplication and identify its base and exponent.
  • Use powers of ten in expanded form and return to standard form.
  • Recognise squares and cubes, and find square roots and cube roots.
  • Apply the order of operations, including brackets, indices and roots.
  • Substitute values into expressions and formulas containing powers.
  • Compare quantities written as powers and justify the comparison.

Success criteria

  • I can expand and evaluate a power without reading the exponent as a multiplier.
  • I can explain why a1=aa^1=aa1=a and, for a≠0a\neq0a=0, a0=1a^0=1a0=1.
  • I can move between standard form and expanded form with powers of ten.
  • I can reverse squaring and cubing with roots.
  • I can show one operation per line and respect brackets.
  • I can explain how brackets change the base of a power.

Ready check

Try these without a calculator. They check multiplication, place value and brackets.

  1. 2.R1Calculate 6 × 7 and 9 × 9.Ready
  2. 2.R2Write 4,000 + 500 + 30 + 6 as a single number.Ready
  3. 2.R3Calculate 12 + 3 × 4.Ready
  4. 2.R4Write 3 × 3 × 3 as a product and evaluate it.Ready
  5. 2.R5What is the area of a square with side 8 cm?Ready
  6. 2.R6Insert brackets so that 2 + 4 × 3 has the value 18.Ready
How to use this chapter

Try the guided practice immediately after the matching example. Use the diagrams to explain what the notation means. Answers and student-facing reasoning are at the back of this proof. If more than two ready-check items are incorrect, review multiplication facts and brackets before continuing.

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 2 · Powers, expanded form and order of operations
Chapter 2 · Investigation · before 2.1

Investigate · How many factors?

Your task

Write each power as repeated multiplication, then evaluate it. Continue the table to 2^7.

PowerRepeated multiplicationValue
2^1
2^2
2^3
2^4
2^5
7^1
5^0

What do you notice?

  • What pattern connects each row to the row above it?
  • Why is 5^0 defined to be 1 rather than 0?
Observation. The exponent counts how many times the base is used as a factor. Each step down divides by the base, so continuing that pattern below 2^1 gives 2^0 = 1; the same argument gives 5^0 = 1 for any nonzero base.
Mathematical conclusion

Index notation records two things: the base (the repeated factor) and the exponent (the number of copies). An exponent of 1 means one factor, and a nonzero base to the power 0 is defined to be 1.

Chapter 2 · 2.1 · From repeated multiplication to powers

The exponent counts factors

Writing 3×3×3×33\times3\times3\times33×3×3×3 is correct but long. Index notation records two things: the repeated factor, called the base, and the number of copies, called the exponent or index.

Worked example 1

Write each power as repeated multiplication and evaluate it: 252^525, 525^252, 10410^4104, 434^343.

  1. 25=2×2×2×2×2=322^5=2\times2\times2\times2\times2=3225=2×2×2×2×2=32.
  2. 52=5×5=255^2=5\times5=2552=5×5=25. This is a square.
  3. 104=10×10×10×10=10,00010^4=10\times10\times10\times10=10{,}000104=10×10×10×10=10,000.
  4. 43=4×4×4=644^3=4\times4\times4=6443=4×4×4=64. This is a cube.

Check: the number of factors must equal the exponent.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Chapter 2 · 2.1 · From repeated multiplication to powers

Special cases and common errors

An exponent of 1 means one factor: 71=77^1=771=7. For a nonzero base, an exponent of 0 is defined to be 1. The pattern of dividing by the base explains the convention:

53=125,52=25,51=5,50=15^3=125,\quad 5^2=25,\quad 5^1=5,\quad 5^0=153=125,52=25,51=5,50=1.

Misconception check

34≠3×43^4\neq3\times434=3×4. The exponent tells how many times to use the base as a factor. Likewise, 52=255^2=2552=25, not 10.

Worked example 2

Write each product as a power and evaluate it: 6×6×6×66\times6\times6\times66×6×6×6, 9×99\times99×9, 2×2×2×2×2×2×22\times2\times2\times2\times2\times2\times22×2×2×2×2×2×2.

  1. Four factors of 6: 64=1,2966^4=1{,}29664=1,296.
  2. Two factors of 9: 92=819^2=8192=81.
  3. Seven factors of 2: 27=1282^7=12827=128.

Count the factors before writing the exponent.

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 2 · Powers, expanded form and order of operations
Chapter 2 · Investigation · before 2.2

Investigate · Place value is built from powers of ten

Your task

Complete the table, then write 5,207 and 60.09 using powers of ten.

PlacePowers of tenDigit in 5,207Contribution
Ten thousands10^4
Thousands10^3
Hundreds10^2
Tens10^1
Ones10^0

What do you notice?

  • What happens to the value of a place each time you move one place to the left?
  • Which places are empty in 5,207, and how does expanded form show that?
Observation. Each place is a power of ten: the ones place is 10^0, the tens place is 10^1 and so on. Moving one place left multiplies by 10 and moving one place right divides by 10, so 5,207 = 5×10^3 + 2×10^2 + 0×10^1 + 7×10^0.
Mathematical conclusion

Expanded form with powers of ten exposes every place, including the empty ones, so a number can be rebuilt without losing a zero.

Chapter 2 · 2.2 · Powers of ten and expanded form

Place value is built from powers of ten

The ones place is 10010^0100, the tens place is 10110^1101, the hundreds place is 10210^2102, and so on. Each step left multiplies by 10; each step right divides by 10.

Worked example 3

Write 5,207 in expanded form using powers of ten.

  1. Read the places: 5 thousands, 2 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones.
  2. Replace each place by a power of ten: 5×103+2×102+0×101+7×1005\times10^3+2\times10^2+0\times10^1+7\times10^05×103+2×102+0×101+7×100.
  3. Check: 5,000+200+0+7=5,2075{,}000+200+0+7=5{,}2075,000+200+0+7=5,207.

The zero term contributes nothing but preserves the place structure.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Chapter 2 · 2.2 · Powers of ten and expanded form

Return to standard form without losing zeros

Expanded form is longer than standard form because it exposes the value of every digit. That makes it useful for checking place value and for seeing the effect of multiplying or dividing by 10.

Worked example 4

Write 6×104+0×103+3×102+9×101+0×1006\times10^4+0\times10^3+3\times10^2+9\times10^1+0\times10^06×104+0×103+3×102+9×101+0×100 in standard form. State the value of the digit 3.

  1. Evaluate nonzero terms: 60,00060{,}00060,000, 300300300, 909090.
  2. Keep the empty thousands and ones places: 60,390.
  3. The 3 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 300.

60,390; the digit 3 contributes 300.

Misconception check

10410^4104 is not 40. It is 10×10×10×10=10,00010\times10\times10\times10=10{,}00010×10×10×10=10,000.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Chapter 2 · Investigation · before 2.3

Investigate · Squares, cubes and their reverses

Your task

Complete the table for n = 1 to 6, then use it to find the square root and cube root of 64.

nn²n³
1
2
3
4
5
6

What do you notice?

  • Which numbers in your table are both square numbers and cube numbers?
  • Test the claim “the square root of a sum is the sum of the square roots” on 9 + 16.
Observation. Square numbers grow by consecutive odd numbers (1, 3, 5, 7, …) and cube numbers grow faster. The root symbol reverses the power, but it does not split sums: √25 = 5 while √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7.
Mathematical conclusion

A square number is a whole number multiplied by itself and a cube number is a whole number multiplied by itself twice. Roots reverse powers; they never distribute over addition.

Chapter 2 · 2.3 · Squares, cubes and roots

Models for squares and cubes

A square number is a whole number multiplied by itself. The positive square numbers begin 1, 4, 9, 16, … A cube number is a whole number multiplied by itself twice: 1, 8, 27, 64, …

Worked example 5

Evaluate 12212^2122, 737^373, 81\sqrt{81}81​, 144\sqrt{144}144​ and 643\sqrt[3]{64}364​.

  1. 122=14412^2=144122=144; 73=3437^3=34373=343.
  2. 92=819^2=8192=81, so 81=9\sqrt{81}=981​=9.
  3. 122=14412^2=144122=144, so 144=12\sqrt{144}=12144​=12.
  4. 43=644^3=6443=64, so 643=4\sqrt[3]{64}=4364​=4.

Reverse a root by squaring or cubing the result.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Chapter 2 · 2.3 · Squares, cubes and roots

Roots reverse powers; they do not split sums

The square root symbol asks for the nonnegative value whose square is the number under the root. The cube root asks for the value whose cube is the number. In geometry, roots recover a side or edge from an area or volume.

Worked example 6

A square has area 121 cm². A cube has volume 125 cm³. Find the side or edge. If the cube’s edge doubles, what happens to its volume?

  1. 121=11\sqrt{121}=11121​=11, so the square’s side is 11 cm.
  2. 1253=5\sqrt[3]{125}=53125​=5, so the cube’s edge is 5 cm.
  3. Doubling all three dimensions multiplies volume by 23=82^3=823=8.

The new cube volume is 8 times the original.

Misconception check

36+64=100=10\sqrt{36+64}=\sqrt{100}=1036+64​=100​=10, but 36+64=6+8=14\sqrt{36}+\sqrt{64}=6+8=1436​+64​=6+8=14. A root applies to the whole value underneath it.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 2 · Powers, expanded form and order of operations
Chapter 2 · Investigation · before 2.4

Investigate · Which order?

Your task

Evaluate each expression twice: once left to right, and once using the agreed order of operations.

ExpressionLeft to rightAgreed order
3 + 4 × 2
(3 + 4) × 2
20 − 6 ÷ 3
2 × 3²
12 ÷ (2 + 4)

What do you notice?

  • Which pairs of answers differ, and why?
  • What do brackets tell you to do, and what do they change about the meaning?
Observation. Without an agreed order the same expression can give different answers. Brackets are evaluated first, then indices, then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction: 3 + 4×2 = 11 but (3 + 4)×2 = 14.
Mathematical conclusion

The order of operations is a shared convention that makes one written expression mean exactly one value. Brackets are the tool for changing it deliberately.

Chapter 2 · 2.4 · Order of operations

A shared convention makes expressions readable

Without an agreed order, 2+3×42+3\times42+3×4 could mean 20 or 14. Mathematics uses a convention so that the same expression has the same value for every reader.

PriorityOperationsHow to apply it
1Brackets and grouping symbolsWork from the innermost bracket outwards. A fraction bar groups the numerator and denominator.
2Indices and rootsEvaluate powers and roots before multiplication, division, addition or subtraction.
3Multiplication and divisionSame priority: work left to right.
4Addition and subtractionSame priority: work left to right.
Worked example 7

Evaluate 7+2×327+2\times3^27+2×32, (7+2)×32(7+2)\times3^2(7+2)×32, 24÷4×224\div4\times224÷4×2 and 24÷(4×2)24\div(4\times2)24÷(4×2).

  1. 7+2×9=7+18=257+2\times9=7+18=257+2×9=7+18=25.
  2. 9×9=819\times9=819×9=81.
  3. Left to right: 24÷4=624\div4=624÷4=6, then 6×2=126\times2=126×2=12.
  4. Brackets first: 24÷8=324\div8=324÷8=3.

25, 81, 12, 3.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Practice 2.4 · Order of operations

  1. 2.4.1Evaluate 8 + 2 × 5.Fluency
  2. 2.4.2Evaluate 20 − 3 × 4.Fluency
  3. 2.4.3Evaluate. (a) 6 + 42 (b) (6 + 4)2 (c) 23 + 32Fluency
Chapter 2 · 2.4 · Order of operations

Brackets, fraction bars and the unary minus

Brackets are the writer’s tool for changing the order. A fraction bar acts like brackets around the whole numerator and the whole denominator.

Worked example 8

Evaluate (18−4×2)2÷5(18-4\times2)^2\div5(18−4×2)2÷5 and 36−62+4\frac{36-6}{2+4}2+436−6​.

  1. Inside the bracket: 4×2=84\times2=84×2=8, so 18−8=1018-8=1018−8=10. Then 102÷5=100÷5=2010^2\div5=100\div5=20102÷5=100÷5=20.
  2. Numerator: 36−6=3036-6=3036−6=30. Denominator: 2+4=62+4=62+4=6. Then 30÷6=530\div6=530÷6=5.

20 and 5.

Boundary note

A minus sign in front of a power is not part of the base unless brackets include it: −32=−(32)=−9-3^2=-(3^2)=-9−32=−(32)=−9, while (−3)2=9(-3)^2=9(−3)2=9.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Guided practice · Copy and complete

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Chapter 2 · 2.4 · Order of operations

Diagnose the error, then repair the calculation

When a calculation goes wrong, identify the first line where the convention was broken. Do not only change the final answer.

Incorrect

12+6÷3=18÷3=612+6\div3=18\div3=612+6÷3=18÷3=6

The student added before dividing.

Correct

12+6÷3=12+2=1412+6\div3=12+2=1412+6÷3=12+2=14

Division has higher priority than addition.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 2 · Powers, expanded form and order of operations
Chapter 2 · Investigation · before 2.5

Investigate · Substitute, then simplify

Your task

Take a = 3 and b = 5. Evaluate each expression by substituting first, then check with a second method.

ExpressionSubstitutionValue
2a + 3b
a² + b²
(a + b)²
2^a
ab − a

What do you notice?

  • Compare a² + b² with (a + b)². Why are the answers different?
  • What does 2^a mean when a = 3, and how is it different from 2a?
Observation. Substitution replaces a letter with its value, then the order of operations applies: 2a + 3b = 2×3 + 3×5 = 21. But (a + b)² = 64 while a² + b² = 34, because the brackets are part of the meaning.
Mathematical conclusion

A letter stands for a number. Substitute carefully, write the multiplication signs, and respect brackets — they carry meaning that the shorthand hides.

Chapter 2 · 2.5 · Substitution and expressions with powers

Substitute first, then ask what is squared

A letter stands for a number. Substitution means replacing the letter with its value and evaluating using the order of operations. Keep brackets around the replacement so the structure stays visible.

Worked example 9

Evaluate 3x23x^23x2 and (3x)2(3x)^2(3x)2 when x=4x=4x=4.

  1. 3x2=3×42=3×16=483x^2=3\times4^2=3\times16=483x2=3×42=3×16=48.
  2. (3x)2=(3×4)2=122=144(3x)^2=(3\times4)^2=12^2=144(3x)2=(3×4)2=122=144.
  3. The second expression squares the whole product, so it is three times the first.

48 and 144.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Guided practice · Copy and complete

  1. 2.G3For x = 5, compare 2x2 and (2x)2. For x = 2, compare x2 + 32 and (x + 3)2. Explain what the brackets change.Guided
Criterion AKnowing and understanding

  3. 2.5.3For a = 3 and b = 4, evaluate a2 + b2 and (a + b)2. Are they equal?Fluency
Chapter 2 · 2.5 · Substitution and expressions with powers

Formulas connect powers to measurement

Area and volume formulas use powers because they multiply equal dimensions. A model may use a power to describe growth or motion; always check what the variables and units mean.

Worked example 10

Find the area of a square with s=7s=7s=7 cm, the volume of a cube with s=4s=4s=4 cm, and the model distance d=5t2d=5t^2d=5t2 when t=3t=3t=3.

  1. A=s2=72=49 cm2A=s^2=7^2=49\text{ cm}^2A=s2=72=49 cm2.
  2. V=s3=43=64 cm3V=s^3=4^3=64\text{ cm}^3V=s3=43=64 cm3.
  3. d=5×32=5×9=45 md=5\times3^2=5\times9=45\text{ m}d=5×32=5×9=45 m. The index is evaluated before multiplying by 5.

49 cm², 64 cm³, 45 m. The distance formula is a simplified model.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Reasoning habit

Before calculating, say what the exponent applies to: a single variable, a product, or a sum.

Chapter 2 · 2.5 · Substitution and expressions with powers

Test a transferred rule

A rule that works in one structure may fail in another. Test the claim (a+b)2=a2+b2(a+b)^2=a^2+b^2(a+b)2=a2+b2 before using it.

Worked example 11

Test the claim with a=3,b=4a=3,b=4a=3,b=4, then with a=2,b=5a=2,b=5a=2,b=5.

  1. (3+4)2=49(3+4)^2=49(3+4)2=49, but 32+42=253^2+4^2=2532+42=25.
  2. (2+5)2=49(2+5)^2=49(2+5)2=49, but 22+52=292^2+5^2=2922+52=29.
  3. One counterexample is enough to reject a universal claim.

The claim is false. Brackets change the base of the power.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Chapter review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • In ana^nan, the base is repeated and the exponent counts factors.
  • a1=aa^1=aa1=a; for a≠0a\neq0a=0, a0=1a^0=1a0=1.
  • Powers of ten encode place value.
  • Square roots and cube roots reverse squaring and cubing.
  • Brackets, indices, then multiplication/division left to right, then addition/subtraction left to right.
  • Substitution preserves structure: brackets change the base.

Vocabulary

power · base · exponent · index · square number · cube number · square root · cube root · expanded form · standard form · order of operations · substitution · formula

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 2 · Powers, expanded form and order of operations
Chapter 2 · Action and projects

Project connections

Mathematics becomes service and action when it answers a need that other people have. Each connection below is student-led: choose one, plan it with your teacher and follow your school’s requirements and supervision.

Service as Action

Community need
Younger learners commonly read 3^2 as 3 × 2 and lose marks they do not need to lose.
Mathematical connection
Index notation, powers of ten, roots and the order of operations (sections 2.1–2.5).
Proposed action
Create a set of six “spot the error” cards with worked corrections and run a lunchtime clinic; record which errors recur.
Expected impact
Learners can read index notation correctly and check a calculation using the order of operations.
Student reflection
Log the errors you saw, how you explained each one, and what you would change in the cards.

Community Project connection

Project idea
A school “big numbers” display for the library: storage, population and distance figures written in index notation.
Community need
Large figures are often quoted without units or powers, so they cannot be compared.
Research question
Which school and local figures are easiest to compare when written with powers of ten?
Mathematics
Powers of ten, expanded form, estimation and unit conversion.
Action and outcome
Collect 12 figures, rewrite each with powers of ten, and build a labelled display with sources.
Beneficiaries
Students, library staff and visitors.
Evidence
Source list, rewritten figures with checks, photographs of the display.

Personal Project connection · MYP 5

Personal interest
Computing and how devices report storage.
Learning goal
To explain device storage figures accurately using powers of two.
Product or outcome
A one-page explainer or short video comparing “GB” as advertised and as reported by a device.
Mathematics
Powers of two, index notation, estimation and unit conversion.
Process
Collect device figures, recompute them in bytes, and explain the difference.
Evidence
Product, process journal and an evaluation against the stated learning goal. This is an MYP 5-oriented extension: follow your school's Personal Project requirements and supervision.

Service as Action is not the same as completing an exercise: it requires action that benefits others and a reflection on that action. The Community Project connection suits the MYP community project completed by students finishing MYP in Year 3 or Year 4, and the Personal Project connection is an adaptable MYP 5-oriented extension. They are deliberately different from one another.

Part I · The grammar of number · MYP Year 1 · Chapter 03

Factors, multiples and primes

Factors, multiples and prime products reveal how numbers are built, so exact grouping and shared schedules can be planned and justified.

Inquiry questions
  • Factual: How do you know when a search for factor pairs is complete, and which divisibility tests are shortcuts?
  • Conceptual: Why does every composite number have a prime factor no larger than its square root, and why do different factor trees give the same prime product?
  • Debatable: When is “equal teams” a fair way to organise a group, and when does it exclude someone?
Second editionFairness and development
Chapter 3 · Opener

Factors, multiples and primes

Factors, multiples and prime products reveal how numbers are built, so exact grouping and shared schedules can be planned and justified.

Engagement

Can 192 students be placed into identical mixed teams without leaving anyone out? What must be true about the number of teams?

Learning goals

  • List factors and multiples systematically.
  • Apply divisibility tests and classify primes.
  • Write prime products and find HCF and LCM.
  • Choose a grouping or schedule method and justify it.

MYP lens

Key concept: Relationships

Related concepts: System, Representation

Global context: Fairness and development

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 3 · Factors, multiples and primes
Chapter 3 · Investigation · before 3.1

Investigate · Factor pairs meet

Your task

List the factor pairs of each number, then count the factors. Record the pair where the partners meet.

nFactor pairsNumber of factorsPairs meet at
12
16
36
49
60

What do you notice?

  • Which numbers have an odd number of factors, and what is special about them?
  • How do you know a pair search is finished without testing every number up to n?
Observation. Pairs are listed in order and the search stops when the partners would repeat: 36 = 1×36, 2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6. A repeated partner such as 6×6 is counted once, so square numbers have an odd number of factors.
Mathematical conclusion

A factor divides a number exactly and a multiple is that number times a whole number. Pair searches are systematic, and squares are the numbers whose factor count is odd.

Chapter 3 · Mathematical development

3.1 Factors, multiples and factor pairs

Big idea

Search for factor pairs in order, then stop when the partners would repeat.

A factor divides a positive whole number exactly. A multiple is that number times a whole number. Since 7 × 12 = 84, 7 and 12 are factors of 84, and 84 is a multiple of both.

For 36, the pairs are 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9 and 6 × 6. The repeated 6 is counted once. A pair search is complete when the next possible first factor has already appeared as a partner.

Worked example · Find every factor of 48

Use factor pairs rather than guessing.

  1. 1 × 48, 2 × 24, 3 × 16, 4 × 12 and 6 × 8.
  2. 5 and 7 do not divide 48. The next partner would repeat.
  3. Collect the factors in order.
1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48: ten factors.

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 3 · Factors, multiples and primes
Chapter 3 · Investigation · before 3.2

Investigate · Digit tests as shortcuts

Your task

Test 4,728 against each divisor using only its digits. Record pass or fail, then confirm one result by dividing.

DivisorTest usedPass or failCheck
2
3
4
5
8
9

What do you notice?

  • Which tests use the last digit, and which use a digit sum?
  • 4,728 passes the tests for 2 and 3. What else can you conclude, and why?
Observation. Tests for 2, 5 and 10 use the last digit; tests for 4 and 8 use the last two and three digits because 100 is divisible by 4 and 1,000 by 8; tests for 3 and 9 use the digit sum. Passing 2 and 3 together means 6 also divides the number.
Mathematical conclusion

Digit tests are shortcuts justified by place value. They give evidence, and an exact division confirms it when the stakes are high.

Chapter 3 · Mathematical development

3.2 Divisibility tests

Big idea

Use digit tests as shortcuts, then confirm with an exact multiplication when needed.

Tests for 2, 5 and 10 use the last digit. Tests for 4 and 8 use the last two and three digits because 100 is divisible by 4 and 1,000 by 8.

For 3 and 9, add the digits. A number is divisible by 6 exactly when it is divisible by both 2 and 3. These tests concern positive whole numbers here; a passing test is evidence, not a guess.

Worked example · Test 4,728

Which of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10 divide it?

  1. Last digit 8: passes 2, fails 5 and 10. Digit sum 21: passes 3, fails 9.
  2. Last two digits 28: passes 4. Last three digits 728 = 8 × 91: passes 8.
  3. Passing 2 and 3 means it also passes 6.
2, 3, 4, 6 and 8.

A digit sum divisible by 3 does not prove divisibility by 6: the number must also be even.

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 3 · Factors, multiples and primes
Chapter 3 · Investigation · before 3.3

Investigate · Prime or composite?

Your task

Test each number by dividing only by primes up to its square root. Record the first factor you find, or write “prime”.

n√n (approx.)Primes to testFirst factor or prime
37
51
57
91
97

What do you notice?

  • Which numbers looked prime but were not, and which test caught them?
  • Why is it enough to test primes no larger than √n?
Observation. If n = a × b and both factors were larger than √n, the product would be larger than n, so a composite must have a factor at or below that boundary. Testing only primes is enough: 51 = 3×17, 57 = 3×19 and 91 = 7×13, while 37 and 97 are prime.
Mathematical conclusion

A prime has exactly two positive factors, 1 and itself; 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite. Trial division stops at √n.

Chapter 3 · Mathematical development

3.3 Prime and composite numbers

Big idea

Classify by the number of factors, and stop a prime search at the square-root boundary.

A prime is a whole number greater than 1 with exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself. A composite has more than two. The number 1 has one factor, so it is neither.

To test n, try prime divisors no larger than √n. If n = a × b and both factors exceeded √n, their product would exceed n. Thus a composite must have a factor at or below that boundary.

Worked example · Is 97 prime?

Test only the primes up to √97.

  1. √97 is between 9 and 10, so test 2, 3, 5 and 7.
  2. 97 is not divisible by any of them.
97 is prime.

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 3 · Factors, multiples and primes
Chapter 3 · Investigation · before 3.4

Investigate · Different trees, same primes

Your task

Factorise 60 with two different starting splits, then factorise 84. Write each as a product of primes.

Starting splitTree branchesPrime product
60 = 2 × 30
60 = 6 × 10
84 = 4 × 21
84 = 7 × 12

What do you notice?

  • Do the two trees for 60 give the same prime product? What about the two trees for 84?
  • How do you use index form to write the product more compactly?
Observation. Different starting pairs lead to the same prime factors apart from order: 60 = 2² × 3 × 5 and 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. Index form groups equal primes, and multiplying the prime product checks the original number.
Mathematical conclusion

A factor tree records repeated splitting until every endpoint is prime. The prime factorisation of a number is unique apart from the order of the factors.

Chapter 3 · Mathematical development

3.4 Prime factorisation

Big idea

Break a composite into factors until every branch ends at a prime.

A factor tree records repeated splitting. Different starting pairs can lead to the same prime factors, apart from order. Index form groups equal primes.

For 84, split 84 into 4 × 21, then 4 into 2 × 2 and 21 into 3 × 7. Thus 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. Multiply the prime product to check the original number.

Worked example · Factorise 72

Use a factor tree or repeated division.

  1. 72 = 8 × 9.
  2. 8 = 2³ and 9 = 3².
  3. Check 8 × 9 = 72.
72 = 2³ × 3².

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 3 · Factors, multiples and primes
Chapter 3 · Investigation · before 3.5

Investigate · Shared groups and shared repeats

Your task

Two buses leave together every 12 minutes and every 18 minutes. List the common multiples up to 100 and the common factors of 12 and 18.

QuantityValues up to 100Smallest or largest
Common multiples of 12 and 18
Common factors of 12 and 18
Prime products12 = 2²×3; 18 = 2×3²

What do you notice?

  • Which quantity answers “when do they leave together again?” and which answers “how large can equal teams be?”
  • Check HCF × LCM = 12 × 18 for this pair.
Observation. The common multiples begin 36, 72, so the buses meet again after 36 minutes; the common factors are 1, 2, 3, 6, so the largest equal teams have 6 members. HCF(12, 18) = 6, LCM(12, 18) = 36 and 6 × 36 = 216 = 12 × 18.
Mathematical conclusion

Choose the HCF for the largest equal groups and the LCM for the next shared repeat. For two numbers the HCF and LCM multiply to the product of the numbers.

Chapter 3 · Mathematical development

3.5 Highest common factor and lowest common multiple

Big idea

Choose HCF for largest equal groups and LCM for the next shared repeat.

The highest common factor (HCF) is the largest number dividing each given number. The lowest common multiple (LCM) is the smallest positive number that is a multiple of each.

Using prime products, take the smallest exponent of each shared prime for the HCF and the largest exponent of each prime appearing for the LCM. For 12 = 2² × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3², HCF = 6 and LCM = 36.

Worked example · Ribbons and schedules

48 cm and 60 cm ribbons are cut into the longest equal pieces. Two bells repeat every 15 and 20 minutes.

  1. HCF(48,60) = 12, so pieces are 12 cm long.
  2. There are 4 + 5 = 9 pieces.
  3. LCM(15,20) = 60, so the bells next coincide after 60 minutes.
12 cm, 9 pieces; 60 minutes.

Chapter 3 · Action and projects

Project connections

Mathematics becomes service and action when it answers a need that other people have. Each connection below is student-led: choose one, plan it with your teacher and follow your school’s requirements and supervision.

Service as Action

Community need
Younger learners struggle to organise a fair rota because they cannot spot common factors.
Mathematical connection
Factors, HCF and LCM (sections 3.1 and 3.5).
Proposed action
Design a rota-planning aid for a school club, then teach two feeder classes how to use it with a worked example.
Expected impact
Club organisers can build rotas that treat every member equally and learners can explain the arithmetic.
Student reflection
Record the questions learners asked, how you checked the rota was fair, and what you would simplify.

Community Project connection

Project idea
A “fair share” audit of how school resources are divided between year groups.
Community need
Resources are often shared by custom rather than by a stated rule.
Research question
When resources are divided equally between year groups, which group sizes actually allow an equal share?
Mathematics
Factors, HCF, LCM and prime factorisation.
Action and outcome
Model three real sharing situations, compute the possible equal divisions and present a recommendation.
Beneficiaries
School leadership, club organisers and students.
Evidence
Sharing models, calculations and the final recommendation with its justification.

Personal Project connection · MYP 5

Personal interest
Event organisation and scheduling.
Learning goal
To design a scheduling method that guarantees fair rotation.
Product or outcome
A scheduling tool or guide for a club, sports team or community group.
Mathematics
Factors, HCF, LCM and prime factorisation.
Process
Collect the constraints, compute the possible cycles and test the plan against them.
Evidence
Product, process journal and an evaluation against the stated learning goal. This is an MYP 5-oriented extension: follow your school's Personal Project requirements and supervision.

Service as Action is not the same as completing an exercise: it requires action that benefits others and a reflection on that action. The Community Project connection suits the MYP community project completed by students finishing MYP in Year 3 or Year 4, and the Personal Project connection is an adaptable MYP 5-oriented extension. They are deliberately different from one another.

Part I · The grammar of number · MYP Year 1 · Chapter 04

Fractions and decimals

The same quantity can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a measurement; choosing a representation makes comparison and calculation more reliable.

Inquiry questions
  • Factual: What makes two fractions equivalent, and which representations of the same quantity are exact?
  • Conceptual: Why must parts be the same size before fractions are added, and why can dividing by a proper fraction make an answer larger?
  • Debatable: When is a fraction a better description than a decimal, and when is the reverse true?
Second editionScientific and technical innovation
Chapter 4 · Opener

Fractions and decimals

The same quantity can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a measurement; choosing a representation makes comparison and calculation more reliable.

Engagement

A recipe must serve nine people instead of six. How can every ingredient change proportionally without changing the taste?

Learning goals

  • Simplify and compare fractions.
  • Use all four operations with fractions and decimals.
  • Round with stated precision and convert representations.
  • Scale a recipe and justify exact versus rounded measurements.

MYP lens

Key concept: Relationships

Related concepts: Equivalence, Representation

Global context: Scientific and technical innovation

ATL focus. In order for a student to transfer mathematical knowledge, students must connect representations and apply a known method in a new measurement or recipe context.

Language bank: numerator · denominator · equivalent · simplest form · common denominator · reciprocal · terminating · repeating · precision

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 4 · Fractions and decimals
Chapter 4 · Investigation · before 4.1

Investigate · Same value, different names

Your task

Shade each fraction of the same bar, then write the missing equivalent fractions.

FractionEquivalent with denominator 12Simplest formDecimal
1/2
2/3
3/4
5/6
36/48

What do you notice?

  • What single operation turns 1/2 into 6/12, and why does it not change the value?
  • How do you know 36/48 is not in simplest form?
Observation. Multiplying or dividing the numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number gives an equivalent fraction, because the whole is cut into more, smaller parts. Dividing by the highest common factor gives the simplest form: 36/48 = 3/4.
Mathematical conclusion

Equivalent fractions describe the same quantity with different-sized parts. Simplest form is reached when the numerator and denominator have no common factor greater than 1.

Chapter 4 · Mathematical development

4.1 Equivalent fractions and simplest form

Big idea

Multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number.

Fractions describe equal parts of one whole. 1/2, 2/4 and 4/8 name the same amount when the wholes are the same size. The number of pieces changes, but the covered amount does not.

To simplify, divide top and bottom by a common factor. A fraction is in simplest form when its numerator and denominator have HCF 1.

Worked example · Simplify 36/48

Find a common factor, or divide by the HCF.

  1. HCF(36,48) = 12.
  2. 36÷12 = 3 and 48÷12 = 4.
3/4.

5/8 and 3/5
7/10 and 3/4
4/9 and 5/12
11/20 and 1/2

What do you notice?

  • Which pairs could you decide without any calculation, and why?
  • Did a larger denominator ever mean a larger fraction? Explain what happened.
Observation. A benchmark such as 1/2 settles some pairs immediately (5/8 > 1/2 > 3/5 needs care, but 7/10 > 1/2). A common denominator always works: 2/3 = 10/15 and 3/5 = 9/15. A larger denominator does not mean a larger fraction, because the size of the parts also depends on the numerator.
Mathematical conclusion

Compare fractions with a common whole, then use a benchmark, a common denominator or a common numerator — whichever is quickest for the pair in front of you.

Chapter 4 · Mathematical development

4.2 Comparing and ordering fractions

Big idea

Use a common whole, a common denominator, a benchmark or a common numerator.

With equal denominators, more parts means a larger fraction. With equal numerators, more parts means each part is smaller. For 3/7 and 3/5, fifths are larger than sevenths.

For unlike parts, use a common denominator: 3/4 = 9/12 and 5/6 = 10/12, so 5/6 is larger. A benchmark such as 1/2 can make comparison faster.

Worked example · Order 2/3, 3/5 and 7/10

Use denominator 30.

  1. 2/3 = 20/30; 3/5 = 18/30; 7/10 = 21/30.
3/5 < 2/3 < 7/10.
Chapter 4 · Practice · Criterion A

Criterion A practice · 4.2 Comparing and ordering fractions

Watch for this misconception

A larger denominator does not automatically mean a larger fraction. Always check the numerator and the size of the whole.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Guided practice · first steps

  1. 4.2.1Compare 3/7 and 3/5 using <, > or =.Fluency
  2. 4.2.2Compare 3/4 and 5/6.Fluency

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 4 · Fractions and decimals
Chapter 4 · Investigation · before 4.3

Investigate · Make the parts the same size

Your task

Use a diagram to add 1/2 and 1/3, then check the claim that 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5.

StepWorkingResult
Draw both fractions on the same bar
Rewrite with a common denominator
Add the parts
Compare with 2/5

What do you notice?

  • Why can the denominators not simply be added?
  • How can you tell from the answer alone that 1/2 + 1/3 cannot be 2/5?
Observation. Halves and thirds are different-sized parts, so they must be rewritten with a common denominator: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6, giving 5/6. The result 2/5 is impossible because it is smaller than 1/2, and adding a positive amount to 1/2 must give more than 1/2.
Mathematical conclusion

Addition and subtraction of fractions need parts of the same size. Always rewrite with a common denominator, then combine the numerators.

Chapter 4 · Mathematical development

4.3 Adding and subtracting fractions

Big idea

Make the parts the same size before combining or comparing amounts.

For like denominators, add or subtract numerators and keep the denominator. For unlike denominators, first write equivalent fractions with a common denominator.

Mixed numbers can be handled as whole and fractional parts or as improper fractions. Borrowing one whole means borrowing denominator/denominator, not 1/10.

Worked example · Add 3/4 and 5/6

Use denominator 12.

  1. 3/4 = 9/12 and 5/6 = 10/12.
  2. 9/12 + 10/12 = 19/12.
19/12 = 1 7/12.
Chapter 4 · Practice · Criterion A

Criterion A practice · 4.3 Adding and subtracting fractions

Watch for this misconception

Do not add denominators: 1/2 + 1/3 is not 2/5. It must be more than 1/2.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Guided practice · first steps

  1. 4.3.1Calculate 3/8 + 1/8 and 7/9 − 2/9.Fluency
  2. 4.3.2Calculate 3/4 + 5/6.Fluency

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 4 · Fractions and decimals
Chapter 4 · Investigation · before 4.4

Investigate · A fraction of a fraction

Your task

Shade 1/2 of a bar, then 1/3 of the shaded part. Afterwards, work out how many halves fit into 2/3.

TaskModelCalculationResult
1/2 of 1/3
2/3 of 3/4
2/3 ÷ 1/2
3/4 ÷ 2/3

What do you notice?

  • What do you notice about the numerators and denominators when you multiply?
  • Why does dividing by 1/2 give an answer larger than 2/3?
Observation. Multiplication takes a fraction of a quantity: numerators multiply and denominators multiply, so 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6. Division asks how many groups fit: 2/3 ÷ 1/2 = 2/3 × 2/1 = 4/3, which is larger than 2/3 because a half is smaller than the amount being shared.
Mathematical conclusion

Use “a fraction of” for multiplication and “how many groups?” for division. Multiplying by a proper fraction shrinks a positive amount; dividing by one can make it larger.

Chapter 4 · Mathematical development

4.4 Multiplying and dividing fractions

Big idea

Use “a fraction of” for multiplication and “how many groups?” for division.

To multiply fractions, multiply numerators and denominators: a/b × c/d = ac/bd. An area model shows why: a rectangle split into b by d equal parts has ac shaded parts.

Dividing by a nonzero fraction asks how many of those fractional groups fit. Dividing by c/d is multiplying by d/c. For example, 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 6.

Worked example · Find 2/3 of 3/5

Use a rectangle split into thirds one way and fifths the other.

  1. The whole has 15 equal cells.
  2. The overlap has 2 × 3 = 6 cells.
  3. 6/15 simplifies to 2/5.
2/3 × 3/5 = 2/5.
Chapter 4 · Practice · Criterion A

Criterion A practice · 4.4 Multiplying and dividing fractions

Watch for this misconception

Multiplying by a proper fraction makes a positive amount smaller. Dividing by a proper fraction can make it larger.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 4 · Fractions and decimals
Chapter 4 · Investigation · before 4.5

Investigate · Decimals, place by place

Your task

Order 0.4, 0.35, 0.405 and 0.45, then round 0.995 to two decimal places.

TaskWorkingResult
Order the four decimals
Write them with three decimal places
Round 0.995 to two decimal places
Round 3.4789 to two decimal places

What do you notice?

  • Which digit decides the order when the tenths are equal?
  • Why does 0.995 round to 1.00 rather than to 0.99?
Observation. Comparing from the highest place downwards puts the order at 0.35, 0.4, 0.405, 0.45. Rounding 0.995 to two decimal places looks at the third decimal digit 5, so the hundredths digit rounds up from 9 to 10 and the carry travels left, giving 1.00.
Mathematical conclusion

Decimals are compared place by place and rounded at the requested stage only. A carry can travel through a run of 9s, so keep every digit until the final step.

Chapter 4 · Mathematical development

4.5 Decimal place value, ordering and rounding

Big idea

Read place value, compare from left to right and round only at the requested stage.

Digits right of the decimal point represent tenths, hundredths, thousandths and so on. Trailing zeros can record precision: 0.40 and 0.4 have equal value but different stated precision.

Compare equal place values from left to right. To round, inspect the next digit: 0–4 rounds down, 5–9 rounds up. Keep trailing zeros when they show the requested decimal places.

Worked example · Round 0.995 to two decimal places

The third decimal digit is 5.

  1. The hundredths digit 9 rounds up and carries through the tenths digit.
  2. Write two digits after the point.
1.00.
Chapter 4 · Practice · Criterion A

Criterion A practice · 4.5 Decimal place value, ordering and rounding

Watch for this misconception

0.35 is larger than 0.4? Compare tenths first: 3 tenths is less than 4 tenths. Length in digits is not size.

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Criterion AKnowing and understanding

Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 4 · Fractions and decimals
Chapter 4 · Investigation · before 4.6

Investigate · A fraction bar means division

Your task

Convert each fraction to a decimal and describe what happens to the digits.

FractionDivisionDecimalStops or repeats?
3/8
1/3
7/40
5/6
2/7

What do you notice?

  • Which fractions give a decimal that stops, and which repeat?
  • How could you predict the behaviour before dividing?
Observation. 3/8 = 0.375 and 7/40 = 0.175 stop, while 1/3 = 0.333…, 5/6 = 0.8333… and 2/7 = 0.285714… repeat. In simplest form, a fraction stops exactly when its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5.
Mathematical conclusion

A fraction bar is a division instruction. Some quotients terminate and some repeat, and the prime factors of the denominator predict which.

Chapter 4 · Mathematical development

4.6 Fractions, decimals and measurement

Big idea

A fraction bar means division; choose the representation that makes the task clearer.

To convert a fraction to a decimal, divide numerator by denominator, or rewrite with denominator 10, 100 or 1,000 when possible. 3/8 = 0.375.

A reduced fraction terminates exactly when its denominator has no prime factors except 2 and 5. Otherwise its decimal repeats: 1/3 = 0.333…. Use an exact fraction when a rounded decimal would hide the value.

Worked example · Compare 3/8 inch and 0.4 inch

Convert to the same representation.

  1. 3/8 = 0.375.
  2. 0.4 = 0.400.
0.4 inch is larger by 0.025 inch.

A calculator display is often rounded. 0.333 is an approximation to 1/3, not exactly equal to it.

Check your progress

Work through the checklist without looking back. Anything you cannot do yet is a target for the mixed practice.

I can now

  • I can find equivalent fractions and write a fraction in simplest form.
  • I can compare and order fractions using a benchmark or a common denominator.
  • I can add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions and justify each method.
  • I can move between fractions and decimals and choose the better representation for a task.

ATL focus. In order for a student to transfer mathematical knowledge, students must connect representations and apply a known method in a new measurement or recipe context.
Part I · The grammar of numberChapter 4 · Fractions and decimals
Chapter 4 · Action and projects

Project connections

Mathematics becomes service and action when it answers a need that other people have. Each connection below is student-led: choose one, plan it with your teacher and follow your school’s requirements and supervision.

Service as Action

Community need
Younger learners often add denominators when adding fractions, and the error persists without a visual model.
Mathematical connection
Equivalent fractions, comparison and addition (sections 4.1–4.3).
Proposed action
Build a set of bar and area models, then run a workshop that starts from the misconception and corrects it with a diagram.
Expected impact
Learners can explain why parts must be the same size before adding, and can check an answer with a benchmark.
Student reflection
Record the misconceptions you met, the model that worked best, and how you checked understanding.

Community Project connection

Project idea
A community kitchen scaling guide for local dishes.
Community need
Recipes are written for fixed numbers of people, so households rescale them unsafely.
Research question
How can a scaling guide keep proportions exact for the dish sizes actually cooked locally?
Mathematics
Equivalent fractions, multiplication of fractions and measurement.
Action and outcome
Collect 6 local recipes, produce a scaling table for 4, 6, 9 and 12 servings, and test two recipes.
Beneficiaries
Families, community cooks and school catering staff.
Evidence
Recipe sources, scaling tables with checks, and photographs of the tested dishes.

Personal Project connection · MYP 5

Personal interest
Cooking, nutrition or food technology.
Learning goal
To build a reliable scaling method for recipes.
Product or outcome
A scaling guide or calculator for a set of recipes.
Mathematics
Fractions, equivalence, multiplication and division of fractions.
Process
Collect recipes, compute scaled quantities, test the results and evaluate the accuracy.
Evidence
Product, process journal and an evaluation against the stated learning goal. This is an MYP 5-oriented extension: follow your school's Personal Project requirements and supervision.

Service as Action is not the same as completing an exercise: it requires action that benefits others and a reflection on that action. The Community Project connection suits the MYP community project completed by students finishing MYP in Year 3 or Year 4, and the Personal Project connection is an adaptable MYP 5-oriented extension. They are deliberately different from one another.

Part II · Parts and proportions · MYP Year 1 · Chapter 05

Percentages and applications

Percentages express change and comparison relative to a whole; identifying that whole makes financial and fairness decisions more reliable.

Inquiry questions
  • Factual: What does “per cent” mean, and how do you convert between fractions, decimals and percentages?
  • Conceptual: Why do successive percentage changes not simply add, and why does every percentage need a stated whole?
  • Debatable: When does a discount advertisement mislead, even when every number on it is correct?
Second editionFairness and development
Chapter 5 · Opener

Percentages and applications

Percentages express change and comparison relative to a whole; identifying that whole makes financial and fairness decisions more reliable.

Engagement

Two shops advertise different discount sequences. Which offer is genuinely cheaper, and what must a price card make clear?

Learning goals

  • Convert between fractions, decimals and percentages.
  • Find percentages and percentage changes.
  • Use multipliers for successive changes.
  • Interpret discounts, taxes, costs and profit in a budget.

MYP lens

Key concept: Change

Related concepts: Quantity, Proportion

Global context: Fairness and development

ATL focus. In order for a student to think critically, students must identify the reference quantity, test a claim with calculations and explain the limits of a financial decision.

Language bank: per cent · reference amount · multiplier · percentage change · discount · tax · revenue · cost · gross profit · net profit
