Part II · Parts and proportionsChapter 5 · Percentages and applications
Chapter 5 · Investigation · before 5.1

Investigate · Out of one hundred

Your task

Shade each percentage on a 100-square grid, then write it as a fraction in simplest form and as a decimal.

PercentageSquares shadedFractionDecimal
25%
30%
60%
12.5%
7%

What do you notice?

  • What does the grid make obvious that the symbol % hides?
  • Which conversion did you use most often, and why?
Observation. A 100-square grid shows that a percentage is a number of parts out of 100, so 25% = 25/100 = 1/4 = 0.25 and 12.5% = 12.5/100 = 1/8 = 0.125. Dividing by 100 converts a percentage to a decimal.
Mathematical conclusion

“Per cent” means “out of one hundred”. Percentages, fractions and decimals are three representations of the same quantity, and the grid makes the equivalence visible.

Chapter 5 · Mathematical development

5.1 Per cent and equivalent representations

Big idea

Read “per cent” as “out of one hundred”, then connect fractions, decimals and percentages.

A percentage is a ratio with denominator 100. 37% means 37/100 = 0.37. A percentage can exceed 100 when the amount is more than the reference whole.

To write a fraction as a percentage, find an equivalent fraction out of 100 or multiply by 100%. To write a percentage as a fraction, put it over 100 and simplify.

Worked example · Connect 3/5, 0.6 and 60%

Scale the fraction to hundredths.

  1. 3/5 = 60/100.
  2. 60/100 = 0.60 = 60%.
All three name the same proportion.

Percentages compare to a stated whole. 50% of different totals need not be equal amounts.

Part II · Parts and proportionsChapter 5 · Percentages and applications
Chapter 5 · Investigation · before 5.2

Investigate · A percentage needs a whole

Your task

Find each percentage of each amount. Then compare your two answers for 20%.

PercentageOf 50Of 200Of 1,250
10%
20%
5%
12.5%
1%

What do you notice?

  • Why are the two answers for 20% different even though the percentage is the same?
  • Which building-block percentages did you use to find 5% and 12.5%?
Observation. A percentage is not an amount until its whole is known: 20% of 50 is 10 while 20% of 200 is 40. Building blocks make the work easier: 10% then halve for 5%, and 10% plus a quarter of it for 12.5%, so 12.5% of 320 = 40.
Mathematical conclusion

Translate “of” into multiplication by the percentage as a fraction or decimal, and always identify the reference amount first.

Chapter 5 · Mathematical development

5.2 Finding a percentage of a quantity

Big idea

Translate “of” into multiplication and identify the reference amount first.

p% of A means p/100 × A. Useful benchmarks are 10% (divide by 10), 1% (divide by 100), 50% (halve) and 25% (quarter). Build other percentages from these.

For 15% of 240, find 10% = 24 and 5% = 12, then add: 36. Or use the multiplier 0.15 × 240 = 36.

Worked example · Find 12.5% of 320

Use a fraction benchmark.

  1. 12.5% = 1/8.
  2. 320 ÷ 8 = 40.
40.

Chapter 5 · Investigation · before 5.3

Investigate · Do two discounts add?

Your task

Apply 20% off and then 10% off to a 250 XOF price (simulated prices). Compare the result with a single 30% discount.

StepCalculationPriceMultiplier
Original1
After 20% off
After a further 10% off
Single 30% off

What do you notice?

  • What single multiplier equals the two discounts together?
  • Which offer is cheaper, and by how much?
Observation. The multipliers compose: 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, so two successive discounts of 20% and 10% leave 72% of the price, which is 180 XOF. A single 30% discount leaves 70%, which is 175 XOF, so the single discount is cheaper by 5 XOF.
Mathematical conclusion

Successive percentage changes multiply, because the second change uses a new base. The combined change is not the sum of the two percentages.

Chapter 5 · Mathematical development

5.3 Percentage increase and decrease

Big idea

Find the change from the original amount, or use a single multiplier.

An increase of p% uses multiplier 1 + p/100; a decrease uses 1 − p/100. The original amount is the reference unless the question says otherwise.

Percentage change = change/original × 100%. A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease uses 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, ending at 96% of the start.

Worked example · £250 with 20% off, then 10% off

Apply each multiplier to the current price.

  1. 250 × 0.8 = 200.
  2. 200 × 0.9 = 180.
  3. A single 30% discount would give 175.
£180; total discount 28%, not 30%.

Criterion A practice · 5.3 Percentage increase and decrease

Watch for this misconception

The second percentage uses a new base. Do not add successive percentage changes unless they apply to the same unchanged whole.

Part II · Parts and proportionsChapter 5 · Percentages and applications
Chapter 5 · Investigation · before 5.4

Investigate · Revenue, cost and profit

Your task

Complete the budget for a market stall (simulated figures), then express each line as a percentage of revenue.

LineAmount (XOF)Percentage of revenue
Revenue480100%
Goods cost264
Gross profit
Fixed costs90
Net profit

What do you notice?

  • Which percentage base did you use for each line, and why does it matter?
  • What happens to the net profit percentage if fixed costs rise to 140 XOF?
Observation. Gross profit is revenue minus goods cost: 480 − 264 = 216, which is 45% of revenue. Net profit also subtracts fixed costs: 216 − 90 = 126, which is 26.25% of revenue. If fixed costs rise to 140, net profit falls to 76, or about 15.8%.
Mathematical conclusion

Separate revenue, costs and profit, and apply each percentage to the correct base. A percentage without its denominator cannot be interpreted.

Chapter 5 · Mathematical development

5.4 Discounts, taxes, profit and budgets

Big idea

Separate revenue, costs and profit; apply percentages to the correct line of a budget.

A discount reduces a marked price. A tax or tip usually increases a stated base. Revenue is money received; cost is money spent; profit is revenue minus all relevant costs.

For a budget, calculate each line, then add. Whole-item purchases may require rounding up. A lower unit price is not automatically a better decision if extra stock cannot be sold.

Worked example · A market-stall budget

Sell 20 honey jars at £8.10, 36 soaps at £3 and 25 jams at £5.

  1. Revenue = 162 + 108 + 125 = £395.
  2. Goods cost = 20×6 + 36×2.50 + 25×3.20 = £290.
  3. Fixed costs = 45 + 18 = £63.
Net profit = 395 − 290 − 63 = £42.

Part II · Parts and proportionsChapter 5 · Percentages and applications
Chapter 5 · Action and projects

Project connections

Mathematics becomes service and action when it answers a need that other people have. Each connection below is student-led: choose one, plan it with your teacher and follow your school’s requirements and supervision.

Service as Action

Community need
Families in the school community compare discount offers without a shared method.
Mathematical connection
Percentages, multipliers and profit (sections 5.1–5.4).
Proposed action
Produce a one-page “which offer is cheaper?” guide in plain language and present it at a parents' evening.
Expected impact
Families can compare successive discounts and spot a misleading base.
Student reflection
Record the questions asked, the examples you used and how you checked that the guide was understood.

Community Project connection

Project idea
A transparent pricing display for a school fair or community market stall.
Community need
Stall prices are often advertised with discounts but no stated base.
Research question
How can a stall display prices so that every customer can check the discount?
Mathematics
Percentages, multipliers, revenue, cost and profit.
Action and outcome
Design and run a stall with price cards showing base, discount and final price, then report revenue and profit.
Beneficiaries
Customers, stall volunteers and the school fund.
Evidence
Price cards, sales records and a short report with percentages of revenue.

Personal Project connection · MYP 5

Personal interest
Small business, retail or personal finance.
Learning goal
To build a pricing model that stays profitable under discounts.
Product or outcome
A pricing and discount planner for a small enterprise or fundraiser.
Mathematics
Percentages, multipliers, revenue, cost and profit.
Process
Set a cost base, model discount options, test the plan and evaluate the outcome.
Evidence
Product, process journal and an evaluation against the stated learning goal. This is an MYP 5-oriented extension: follow your school's Personal Project requirements and supervision.

Service as Action is not the same as completing an exercise: it requires action that benefits others and a reflection on that action. The Community Project connection suits the MYP community project completed by students finishing MYP in Year 3 or Year 4, and the Personal Project connection is an adaptable MYP 5-oriented extension. They are deliberately different from one another.

Part III · Patterns and symbols · MYP Year 1 · Chapter 06

Patterns, expressions and equations

A pattern can be described by a rule; expressions, equations and formulas make the relationship precise and allow prediction and design.

Inquiry questions
  • Factual: How do you describe how a pattern grows, and what does a letter in an expression stand for?
  • Conceptual: Why does expanding brackets use the distributive law, and why must an equation stay balanced?
  • Debatable: Is a rule that fits the first few terms of a pattern proved, or only suggested?
Second editionScientific and technical innovation
Chapter 6 · Opener

Patterns, expressions and equations

A pattern can be described by a rule; expressions, equations and formulas make the relationship precise and allow prediction and design.

Engagement

How can a gardener order exactly the right number of border slabs for a square pond of any whole-number side length?

Learning goals

  • Describe and generalise a growing pattern.
  • Substitute into expressions and simplify or expand.
  • Solve linear equations and check solutions.
  • Use formulas and budget constraints in a design.

MYP lens

Key concept: Relationships

Related concepts: Pattern, Equivalence

Global context: Scientific and technical innovation

ATL focus. In order for a student to transfer mathematical knowledge, students must move between a diagram, a table, a rule and an equation, then check the result in context.

Language bank: sequence · term · position · variable · expression · coefficient · like terms · expand · factorise · equation · formula · solution

Part III · Patterns and symbolsChapter 6 · Patterns, expressions and equations
Chapter 6 · Investigation · before 6.1

Investigate · Growing patterns

Your task

Draw or build stages 1 to 4 of the matchstick chain, then complete the table.

Stage n1234510
Matches
Change from previous stage—

What do you notice?

  • What stays the same at every stage, and what changes?
  • Write a rule for the number of matches at stage n and test it on stage 5.
Observation. Each stage adds the same number of matches, so the growth is linear. If the first stage uses 4 matches and each later stage adds 3, the rule is matches = 3n + 1, which gives 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 and 31 for stages 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10.
Mathematical conclusion

Describe how a pattern grows, then connect the picture to a rule for any position. A rule that explains the structure can be trusted beyond the drawn stages.

Chapter 6 · Mathematical development

6.1 Patterns, rules and sequences

Big idea

Describe how a pattern grows, then connect the picture to a rule for any position.

A sequence has terms in positions 1, 2, 3, …. A term-to-term rule says how to get the next term. A position-to-term rule uses the position n to find a term directly.

For 4, 7, 10, 13, …, add 3 each time. The nth term is 3n + 1 because position 1 gives 4. A rule must match every given term, not only the first.

Worked example · A growing matchstick chain

One square uses 4 matches; each extra square shares one side and adds 3.

  1. n squares use 4 + 3(n−1) matches.
  2. Simplify to 3n + 1.
  3. For 10 squares: 31 matches.
3n + 1; 31 matches for 10 squares.

Part III · Patterns and symbolsChapter 6 · Patterns, expressions and equations
Chapter 6 · Investigation · before 6.2

Investigate · A letter stands for a number

Your task

Take a = 4 and b = 3. Evaluate each expression by substituting first, then check with a second method.

ExpressionAfter substitutionValue
2a + 3b
ab
a²
(a + b)²
2^a

What do you notice?

  • What is the difference between ab and a + b? Between a² and 2a?
  • Why do the answers for a² + b² and (a + b)² differ?
Observation. Substitution replaces each letter with its value, then the order of operations applies: 2a + 3b = 2×4 + 3×3 = 17 and ab = 12. But a² + b² = 25 while (a + b)² = 49, because the brackets are part of the meaning.
Mathematical conclusion

A letter stands for a number. Write multiplication signs when substituting, and treat brackets as instructions that change the value.

Chapter 6 · Mathematical development

6.2 Expressions and substitution

Big idea

A letter stands for a number. Replace it carefully and follow the order of operations.

An expression such as 3n + 5 combines numbers, letters and operations. It has no equals sign. A term is a part added or subtracted; a coefficient multiplies a letter.

To evaluate, substitute the value and use brackets where needed. If n=4, 3n+5 = 3×4+5 = 17. If x=−2, x² = 4 but −x² = −4.

Worked example · Evaluate 2a + 3b

Let a=5 and b=2.

  1. 2×5 + 3×2.
  2. 10 + 6.
16.

Part III · Patterns and symbolsChapter 6 · Patterns, expressions and equations
Chapter 6 · Investigation · before 6.3

Investigate · Combine and expand

Your task

Simplify 4x + 3 + 2x − 5, then expand (x + 2)(x + 3) using an area model.

TaskWorkingResult
Collect like terms in 4x + 3 + 2x − 5
Area model for (x + 2)(x + 3)
Expand 3(x + 4)
Compare x + x and x × x

What do you notice?

  • Which terms may be combined, and which may not?
  • How does the area model show that (x + 2)(x + 3) = x² + 5x + 6?
Observation. Only like terms combine: 4x + 2x = 6x and 3 − 5 = −2, giving 6x − 2. An area model splits a rectangle into four parts, giving x² + 3x + 2x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6, and 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12 by the distributive law.
Mathematical conclusion

Combine only like terms and use the distributive law to remove brackets. Addition and multiplication are different operations: x + x = 2x while x × x = x².

Chapter 6 · Mathematical development

6.3 Simplifying and expanding expressions

Big idea

Combine only like terms; use the distributive law to remove brackets.

Like terms have the same letter part. 3x + 5x = 8x, but 3x + 5 cannot be combined into one term. Rearranging terms does not change their value.

Expanding uses a(b+c)=ab+ac. For 3(2x+4), multiply every term inside: 6x+12. Factorising reverses this: 6x+12 = 3(2x+4).

Worked example · Simplify 4x + 3 + 2x − 5

Group like terms.

  1. 4x+2x = 6x.
  2. 3−5 = −2.
6x − 2.

Part III · Patterns and symbolsChapter 6 · Patterns, expressions and equations
Chapter 6 · Investigation · before 6.4

Investigate · Balanced equations

Your task

Solve 4n + 4 = 44 using the balance model, then check by substitution. Repeat with 3n + 5 = 20.

StepBalance actionResult
Start4n + 4 = 44
Remove 4 from each side
Divide each side by 4
Check by substitution

What do you notice?

  • What must happen to both sides of the balance at every step?
  • Why is subtracting 5 before dividing by 3 necessary in 3n + 5 = 20?
Observation. An equation states that two expressions are equal, so the same operation must be applied to both sides: 4n + 4 = 44 gives 4n = 40 and n = 10, and 4(10) + 4 = 44 confirms it. In 3n + 5 = 20, dividing by 3 first would leave n + 5/3, so the 5 is removed first.
Mathematical conclusion

Keep both sides balanced, apply inverse operations in a sensible order, and always substitute the solution back to check.

Chapter 6 · Mathematical development

6.4 Equations, formulas and checking solutions

Big idea

An equation states equality. Keep both sides balanced, then substitute the solution to check.

To solve, undo operations in reverse order. For 3n+5=20, subtract 5 from both sides, then divide by 3: n=5. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

A formula connects quantities, such as C=3+2d. To find d when C=19, solve 19=3+2d. A solution should satisfy the original equation and make sense in context.

Worked example · Solve 4n + 4 = 44

Undo addition, then multiplication.

  1. 4n = 40.
  2. n = 10.
  3. Check: 4×10+4 = 44.
n=10.
Chapter 6 · Practice · Criterion A

Criterion A practice · 6.4 Equations, formulas and checking solutions

Watch for this misconception

Do not divide only one term. In 3n+5=20, subtract 5 before dividing the whole side by 3.

Part III · Patterns and symbolsChapter 6 · Patterns, expressions and equations
Chapter 6 · Action and projects

Project connections

Mathematics becomes service and action when it answers a need that other people have. Each connection below is student-led: choose one, plan it with your teacher and follow your school’s requirements and supervision.

Service as Action

Community need
Younger learners can compute but cannot explain why a pattern rule works.
Mathematical connection
Patterns, expressions and equations (sections 6.1–6.4).
Proposed action
Create a set of pattern cards with a “show the structure” challenge and run a workshop that requires learners to justify, not just extend, a pattern.
Expected impact
Learners can describe growth, write a rule and defend it with the structure of the pattern.
Student reflection
Record which justifications learners found convincing and how you prompted them to go further.

Community Project connection

Project idea
A costing model for a school fundraiser stall.
Community need
Fundraisers often set prices by guesswork, so the profit is unpredictable.
Research question
What price and volume does a stall need in order to cover its costs and reach a target profit?
Mathematics
Expressions, substitution, formulas and solving equations.
Action and outcome
Build a cost model, solve for the break-even point and present a recommended price.
Beneficiaries
Stall volunteers, the school fund and customers.
Evidence
Cost model, break-even calculation and the final recommendation.

Personal Project connection · MYP 5

Personal interest
Design, engineering or gaming mechanics.
Learning goal
To model a real or designed system with a formula and solve for an unknown.
Product or outcome
A model or simulator for a system of personal interest.
Mathematics
Patterns, expressions, formulas and equations.
Process
Identify the variables, build the formula, test it against data and solve for a target.
Evidence
Product, process journal and an evaluation against the stated learning goal. This is an MYP 5-oriented extension: follow your school's Personal Project requirements and supervision.

Service as Action is not the same as completing an exercise: it requires action that benefits others and a reflection on that action. The Community Project connection suits the MYP community project completed by students finishing MYP in Year 3 or Year 4, and the Personal Project connection is an adaptable MYP 5-oriented extension. They are deliberately different from one another.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measure · MYP Year 1 · Chapter 07

Lines, angles, triangles and constructions

A single straight line contains 180°, and a full turn contains 360°. From those two facts, and one statement about parallel lines, an entire system of shape reasoning follows. Constructions turn that reasoning into a repeatable physical procedure.

Key concept · RelationshipsRelated · SpaceRelated · RepresentationContext · Orientation in space and time
Inquiry

A workshop needs a triangular roof truss with equal slopes and a horizontal collar beam. Which angles must the carpenter set, how can the shape be checked without measuring every angle, and how can a full-size template be reproduced exactly?

MYP Mathematics 1Student coursebook · Prototype
Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7 · Opener

Reasoning with straight lines

Geometry begins with a few reliable facts and becomes powerful when those facts are connected. In this chapter you will name angle relationships, explain triangle and polygon sums, and use equal-radius constructions to force a property rather than guess it.

Engagement

Before cutting timber, a carpenter can test a design with a scale drawing. Which measurements are enough to guarantee the shape? Which checks protect against a drawing that only looks correct?

Inquiry questions

  • Factual: What do angles on a straight line and around a point add to?
  • Conceptual: Why must the two shorter sides of a triangle together exceed the longest side?
  • Debatable: When is a construction reliable enough to build from?

Learning goals

  • Use angle facts on lines, at points and with parallel lines.
  • Reason with triangle and polygon angle sums.
  • Apply the triangle inequality and regular-polygon facts.
  • Construct perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors and SSS triangles.

MYP lens

Key concept: Relationships

Related concepts: Space, Representation

Global context: Orientation in space and time

Criteria: A, B, C and D in separate tasks

ATL focus. In order for a student to think creatively and critically, students must choose an appropriate geometric fact or construction, test a design and explain why the method is reliable.

Language bank: acute · right · obtuse · reflex · vertically opposite · corresponding · alternate · co-interior · isosceles · exterior angle · polygon · perpendicular bisector · angle bisector · construction

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7 · How to use the practice

Six kinds of mathematical thinking

The practice is organised by concept, then by the kind of thinking it develops. The labels describe the task, not a separate mark scheme.

Understand

Identify, classify, state, complete and interpret definitions, notation and properties.

Fluency

Calculate, solve, complete diagrams and use procedures accurately.

Reasoning

Justify, compare methods, find errors and explain why a statement is true or false.

Investigation

Observe, organise evidence, make conjectures, test them and draw conclusions.

Application

Use mathematics in design, measurement and everyday contexts, then interpret the result.

Challenge

Combine ideas, consider alternatives and explain deeper relationships.
Working space

Use the space provided for diagrams, equations and checks. Construction tasks ask you to draw in your notebook at the stated size; printed figures are models, not always full-size templates.

ATL evidence. As you work, record one place where you chose a method, one place where you tested a result, and one place where you explained why the method is reliable.
Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7 · Mathematical development

7.1 Lines, angles and angle facts

Name the relationship first: straight line, full turn, vertically opposite or right angle.

An angle measures a turn. A half-turn along a straight line is 180°, so adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary. A full turn about a point is 360°. When two straight lines cross, vertically opposite angles are equal.

Straight line: the two angles complete 180°.
Full turn: the four angles complete 360°.

Key idea

Straight line: 180°. Full turn: 360°. Vertically opposite: equal. Right angle: 90°. Complementary angles sum to 90°; supplementary angles sum to 180°. The middle letter of angle ABC names the vertex B.

Common error

Do not swap the totals: a straight line is 180°, a full turn is 360°. Do not treat vertically opposite angles as supplementary; they are equal. The adjacent pair is supplementary.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.1 · Worked example 7.1.1

Missing angle on a straight line

Problem

Two adjacent angles on a straight line are 47° and x. Find x.

Visual representation
Figure 7.1 · The two angles share a vertex and lie on a straight line.
Mathematical reasoning

A straight line is a half-turn, so adjacent angles on it are supplementary: their sum is 180°.

Step-by-step solution
  1. Identify the relationship: the two angles lie on one straight line.
  2. Write the equation: 47° + x = 180°.
  3. Subtract 47° from both sides: x = 180° − 47° = 133°.
  4. Check: 47° + 133° = 180°.
Final answer. x = 133°.

Interpretation. The unknown angle is obtuse. The diagram and the equation agree: the two angles complete a half-turn.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.1 · Worked example 7.1.2

Angles around a point

Problem

Four angles meet at a point: 95°, 120°, 85° and x. Find x.

Visual representation
Figure 7.2 · Four sectors fill one full turn.
Mathematical reasoning

A full turn around a point is 360°. The four angles must fill the turn exactly.

Step-by-step solution
  1. Add the known angles: 95° + 120° + 85° = 300°.
  2. Subtract from the full turn: x = 360° − 300° = 60°.
  3. Check: 95° + 120° + 85° + 60° = 360°.
Final answer. x = 60°.

Interpretation. The missing sector is acute. The visual model shows why the total must be 360°, not 180°.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.1 · Worked example 7.1.3

Vertically opposite angles with algebra

Problem

Two lines cross. Vertically opposite angles are labelled 3x + 10° and x + 50°. Find x and one adjacent angle.

Visual representation
Figure 7.3 · Opposite angles are equal; adjacent angles sum to 180°.
Mathematical reasoning

Vertically opposite angles are equal. Adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary.

Step-by-step solution
  1. Set the opposite angles equal: 3x + 10 = x + 50.
  2. Collect terms: 2x = 40, so x = 20°.
  3. Each marked angle is 3(20) + 10 = 70°.
  4. An adjacent angle is 180° − 70° = 110°. Check: 70° + 110° = 180°.
Final answer. x = 20°; marked angles 70°; adjacent angle 110°.

Interpretation. The algebra confirms the visual symmetry: opposite sectors match, and neighbouring sectors complete a line.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7 · Mathematical development

7.2 Parallel lines and transversals

A transversal crosses two or more lines. When the crossed lines are parallel, the angles fall into equal or supplementary families.

Figure 7.4 · With l parallel to m: corresponding and alternate angles are equal; co-interior angles are supplementary.

Key idea

Corresponding angles sit in the same position at each intersection. Alternate angles lie on opposite sides of the transversal between the parallel lines. Co-interior angles lie on the same side between the parallel lines.

Watch for this misconception

Do not assume lines are parallel or angles equal unless marked or stated. Conversely, equal alternate angles or supplementary co-interior angles can show that two lines are parallel.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7 · Mathematical development

Triangle and exterior-angle facts

Every triangle has angle sum 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.

Equal sides give equal base angles.
Exterior angle = sum of opposite interior angles.

Key idea

Triangles may be classified by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles (acute, right, obtuse). In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal; conversely, equal angles face equal sides. In a right triangle the two acute angles are complementary.

Common error

The exterior angle is equal to the sum of the two opposite interior angles. It is not added to them to make 180°. The adjacent interior angle is the one supplementary to the exterior angle.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.2 · Worked example 7.2.1

Parallel-line angle chase

Problem

Lines l and m are parallel. The marked angle is 68°. Find a, b and c.

Visual representation
Figure 7.5 · Parallel marks justify the angle relationships.
Mathematical reasoning

With parallel lines, alternate angles are equal, co-interior angles are supplementary, and corresponding angles are equal.

Step-by-step solution
  1. a is alternate to 68°, so a = 68°.
  2. b is co-interior with 68°, so b = 180° − 68° = 112°.
  3. c corresponds to the 68° angle (both are in the lower-right position), so c = 68°.
  4. Check: a + b = 68° + 112° = 180°.
Final answer. a = 68°, b = 112°, c = 68°.

Interpretation. The transversal creates two angle families: 68° and 112°. Naming the relationship prevents guessing from appearance.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.2 · Worked example 7.2.2

Exterior angle of a triangle

Problem

An exterior angle of a triangle is 115°. One opposite interior angle is 48°. Find the other opposite interior angle and the adjacent interior angle.

Visual representation
Figure 7.6 · The exterior angle is outside the triangle at the extended base.
Mathematical reasoning

An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. It is supplementary to the interior angle at the same vertex.

Step-by-step solution
  1. Other opposite interior angle = 115° − 48° = 67°.
  2. Adjacent interior angle = 180° − 115° = 65°.
  3. Check the triangle sum: 48° + 67° + 65° = 180°.
Final answer. Other opposite angle 67°; adjacent interior angle 65°.

Interpretation. The exterior angle is larger than either opposite interior angle. The diagram shows which angles belong to the exterior-angle relationship.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.2 · Worked example 7.2.3

Isosceles base angles

Problem

An isosceles triangle has apex angle 40°. Find each base angle.

Visual representation
Figure 7.7 · Equal sides force equal base angles.
Mathematical reasoning

Equal sides have equal opposite angles. The triangle angle sum is 180°.

Step-by-step solution
  1. The tick marks show two equal sides, so the base angles are equal. Call each x.
  2. Write 2x + 40° = 180°.
  3. Then 2x = 140°, so x = 70°.
  4. Check: 70° + 70° + 40° = 180°.
Final answer. Each base angle is 70°.

Interpretation. The equal-side marks are the evidence for equal base angles; the calculation then uses the angle sum.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.2 · Worked example 7.2.4

Why every triangle has angle sum 180°

Problem

Use a line through the apex parallel to the base to explain why the angles of a triangle sum to 180°.

Visual representation
Figure 7.8 · The parallel line transfers the base angles to the apex.
Mathematical reasoning

Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal. Angles on a straight line sum to 180°.

Step-by-step solution
  1. Draw a line through the apex parallel to the base.
  2. The left base angle equals the left angle at the apex (alternate angles). The right base angle equals the right angle at the apex.
  3. The three angles on the straight line through the apex are therefore the three triangle angles.
  4. They sum to 180°, so the triangle angles sum to 180°.
Final answer. A + B + C = 180° for every triangle.

Interpretation. This is a visual argument, not a measurement of one triangle. It explains why the rule is general.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7 · Mathematical development

7.3 Polygons and their angles

A polygon is a closed plane shape made from straight sides. Its interior angle sum depends on the number of sides.

Figure 7.9 · A hexagon splits into four triangles from one vertex.

Choose one vertex and draw diagonals to every non-adjacent vertex. An n-sided polygon divides into n−2 triangles, so its interior angle sum is (n−2)×180°. The exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360°.

Key idea

Interior sum: (n−2)×180°. Exterior sum: 360°. Regular polygon: each exterior = 360°÷n; each interior = 180°−360°÷n.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.3 · Worked example 7.3.1

Missing angle in a quadrilateral

Problem

A quadrilateral has angles 85°, 95°, 110° and x. Find x.

Visual representation
Figure 7.10 · One diagonal divides the quadrilateral into two triangles.
Mathematical reasoning

A quadrilateral can be split into two triangles, so its interior angle sum is 2 × 180° = 360°.

Step-by-step solution
  1. Add the known angles: 85° + 95° + 110° = 290°.
  2. Subtract from 360°: x = 360° − 290° = 70°.
  3. Check: 85° + 95° + 110° + 70° = 360°.
Final answer. x = 70°.

Interpretation. The diagonal in the diagram shows where the 360° comes from: two triangle sums.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.3 · Worked example 7.3.2

Regular polygon from an exterior angle

Problem

A regular polygon has exterior angle 40°. Find the number of sides and each interior angle.

Visual representation
Figure 7.11 · A regular nonagon has nine equal exterior turns.
Mathematical reasoning

The exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360°. In a regular polygon they are equal. Interior and exterior angles at a vertex are supplementary.

Step-by-step solution
  1. Number of sides n = 360° ÷ 40° = 9.
  2. Each interior angle = 180° − 40° = 140°.
  3. Check with the interior-sum formula: (9 − 2) × 180° = 1260°, and 1260° ÷ 9 = 140°.
Final answer. 9 sides; each interior angle 140°.

Interpretation. A small exterior angle means many sides. The polygon is a regular nonagon.

Which lengths close a triangle?

Three strips joined end to end may or may not close a triangle. Predict first, then test. Do not state a rule until the evidence forces it.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7 · Investigation · Discovery

From evidence to a rule

Write your conjecture before comparing it with the formal statement below.

Discovery

The two shorter sides must together be strictly greater than the longest side. If a+b=c, the arcs meet on the base and the triangle has zero area. If a+b<c, the arcs do not meet.

Conclusion

For sides a, b, c with c longest, a triangle exists if and only if a+b>c. The other two inequalities then hold automatically. This is the triangle inequality.

Figure 7.12 · Equality gives a degenerate straight line.
Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.3 · Worked example 7.3.3

Possible third sides

Problem

Two sides of a triangle are 7 cm and 11 cm. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. Find all possible values.

Visual representation
Figure 7.13 · The number line represents 4 < x < 18.
Mathematical reasoning

The third side must be greater than the difference of the other two sides and less than their sum. Endpoints give degenerate cases.

Step-by-step solution
  1. Lower boundary: 11 − 7 = 4, so x > 4.
  2. Upper boundary: 11 + 7 = 18, so x < 18.
  3. Whole-number values are 5, 6, 7, …, 17.
  4. Check endpoints: x = 4 gives 4 + 7 = 11; x = 18 gives 7 + 11 = 18. Both are straight-line cases, not triangles.
Final answer. x = 5, 6, 7, …, 17 cm.

Interpretation. The open circles on the number line show that 4 and 18 are excluded. The integer dots are the possible whole-centimetre lengths.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7 · Mathematical development

7.4 Constructions with ruler and compass

A construction is an argument made with instruments. Each arc records a fixed distance from a named point.

Perpendicular bisector: equidistant from two endpoints.
Angle bisector: equidistant from the two arms.
ConstructionCompass settingHow to test
Perpendicular bisector of ABOne radius greater than half AB, unchanged from A and BCrosses AB at its midpoint and makes 90°
Angle bisectorArc from vertex cuts both arms; same radius from those pointsTwo half-angles are equal
Triangle from three sidesBase equal to one side; radii equal to the other two sidesArcs meet; two shorter sides exceed the longest
Common error

Never change the compass between a pair of arcs. Check the defining property, not the appearance of the drawing.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7 · Mathematical development

Constructing triangles from sides

To construct a triangle from three sides, fix the base and locate the apex with two arcs.

Figure 7.14 · The arc intersection fixes the third vertex.

The triangle inequality predicts whether the arcs meet above the base. If the two shorter sides together equal the longest side, the apex lies on the base; if they are shorter, the arcs do not meet.

Key idea

SSS construction: base AB, arc from A with radius AC, arc from B with radius BC. The intersection is C. Keep the arcs visible as evidence.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.4 · Worked example 7.4.1

Perpendicular bisector

Problem

Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB = 8 cm. State the midpoint length and the check.

Visual representation
Figure 7.15 · The same compass radius is used from both endpoints.
Mathematical reasoning

Points on the perpendicular bisector are equidistant from A and B. Equal-radius arcs locate two such points.

Step-by-step solution
  1. Draw AB = 8 cm.
  2. Choose one radius greater than half of AB, for example 5 cm. Keep it fixed.
  3. Draw arcs from A and from B above and below AB. Label the intersections P and Q.
  4. Draw PQ. It crosses AB at its midpoint M, so AM = MB = 4 cm, and PQ is perpendicular to AB.
Final answer. AM = MB = 4 cm; PQ is perpendicular to AB.

Interpretation. The arcs are evidence: P and Q are each the same distance from A and B, so the line through them is the perpendicular bisector.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.4 · Worked example 7.4.2

Angle bisector

Problem

Bisect a 64° angle with ruler and compasses. Find each half.

Visual representation
Figure 7.16 · The bisector is the ray OR.
Mathematical reasoning

An angle bisector divides an angle into two equal angles. Equal-radius arcs from the arms locate a point on the bisector.

Step-by-step solution
  1. Draw an arc from the vertex O, cutting the arms at P and Q.
  2. With the same radius from P and Q, draw arcs meeting at R.
  3. Draw OR. This is the angle bisector.
  4. Each half is 64° ÷ 2 = 32°. Check: 32° + 32° = 64°.
Final answer. Each half is 32°.

Interpretation. The construction forces equality; measuring is only a check. Do not confuse this with the perpendicular bisector of a segment.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.4 · Worked example 7.4.3

Triangle from three sides (SSS)

Problem

Construct a triangle with sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm.

Visual representation
Figure 7.17 · The arc intersection fixes the third vertex.
Mathematical reasoning

If two sides and the base are fixed, the third vertex is the intersection of two circles/arcs. The triangle inequality predicts whether the arcs meet.

Step-by-step solution
  1. Check: 5 + 6 > 7, so a triangle is possible.
  2. Draw base AB = 7 cm.
  3. From A draw an arc of radius 5 cm; from B draw an arc of radius 6 cm.
  4. Label the intersection C and join AC and BC. Keep the arcs visible.
Final answer. Triangle ABC has AB = 7 cm, AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm.

Interpretation. The arcs locate the only possible apex on each side of the base. The two choices are mirror images.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7.4 · Worked example 7.4.4

Isosceles triangle and a locus

Problem

Construct an isosceles triangle with equal sides 6 cm and base 8 cm. Explain why the perpendicular bisector of the base passes through the apex.

Visual representation
Figure 7.18 · Equal sides place the apex on the perpendicular bisector.
Mathematical reasoning

The apex is equidistant from the base endpoints. The perpendicular bisector is the locus of all points equidistant from the endpoints.

Step-by-step solution
  1. Draw base AB = 8 cm.
  2. With radius 6 cm from A and from B, draw arcs meeting at C.
  3. Join AC and BC. Then AC = BC = 6 cm.
  4. Because C is equidistant from A and B, it lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
Final answer. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through C.

Interpretation. The equal sides are not just a picture feature; they place the apex on a precise locus. This connects construction with reasoning.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 7 · Lines, angles, triangles and constructions
Chapter 7 · Review

Summary and connections

Angle facts

  • Straight line: 180°.
  • Full turn: 360°.
  • Vertically opposite: equal.
  • Parallel lines: corresponding and alternate equal; co-interior supplementary.

Triangles and polygons

  • Triangle sum: 180°.
  • Exterior angle: sum of opposite interior angles.
  • n-gon interior sum: (n−2)×180°.
  • Exterior sum: 360°.

Constructions

  • Perpendicular bisector: equal radii greater than half the segment.
  • Angle bisector: equal arcs from the arms.
  • SSS triangle: arcs meet when the triangle inequality holds.

Inquiry

  • Triangle inequality: two shorter sides > longest.
  • Equality gives a degenerate straight line.
  • Keep arcs visible as evidence.
Connections · Drawing is not proving

A construction is an argument made with instruments. Each arc records a fixed distance from a named point, so the finished drawing already contains evidence: equal radii, equal distances, and a property that can be checked. A picture that looks right is not enough; the defining relationship must hold.

Where this leads: Chapter 8 turns classification into a precise language. Sets describe which objects share a property, and Venn diagrams show relationships of overlap and exclusion. Chapter 9 then measures the shapes whose boundaries you have learned to reason about.

Chapter 7 · Action and projects

Project connections

Mathematics becomes service and action when it answers a need that other people have. Each connection below is student-led: choose one, plan it with your teacher and follow your school’s requirements and supervision.

Service as Action

Community need
A local workshop or school design club produces layouts that cannot be checked before cutting materials.
Mathematical connection
Angle facts, the triangle inequality and ruler-and-compass constructions (sections 7.1–7.4).
Proposed action
Produce a one-page checking card — angle sum, parallel-line test and the triangle inequality — and teach it to the club so every design is checked before cutting.
Expected impact
Designs are checked with measurements rather than by eye, so less material is wasted.
Student reflection
Record which check caught the most errors, how you taught it and what you would add to the card.

Community Project connection

Project idea
A measured plan for a community shade, ramp or garden frame.
Community need
Small community builds are often laid out by eye, so joints do not fit.
Research question
Which measurements guarantee that a triangular frame is rigid and fits its site?
Mathematics
Angle sums, parallel lines, the triangle inequality and constructions.
Action and outcome
Produce a scale drawing and a construction card, then check a prototype with a partner.
Beneficiaries
Community group members and the people who use the structure.
Evidence
Scale drawing, construction card, checking log and photographs of the prototype.

Personal Project connection · MYP 5

Personal interest
Design, carpentry, engineering or architecture.
Learning goal
To produce a design whose geometry can be verified without a protractor.
Product or outcome

Part IV · Shape, structure and measure · MYP Year 1 · Chapter 08

Sets and classification

Sets organise membership and overlap; clear definitions and representations prevent double counting and make survey claims testable.

Inquiry questions
  • Factual: What is the difference between an element of a set and a subset of a set, and what do union and intersection mean?
  • Conceptual: Why must a Venn diagram be filled from the overlap outwards, and how do you classify a number by the sets it belongs to?
  • Debatable: When can a survey category be defined so precisely that its counts can be trusted?

Sets and classification

Sets organise membership and overlap; clear definitions and representations prevent double counting and make survey claims testable.

Engagement

When two groups overlap, what can we know about the missing intersection, and how does that change a decision?

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 8 · Sets and classification
Chapter 8 · Investigation · before 8.1

Investigate · Elements and subsets

Your task

List every subset of {a, b} and of {a, b, c}. Count them and look for a pattern.

SetNumber of elementsNumber of subsetsSubsets
{a}
{a, b}
{a, b, c}
{a, b, c, d} (predict)

What do you notice?

  • How does the number of subsets change when one element is added?
  • Is the empty set a subset of every set? How can you tell from your list?
Observation. A set with 1 element has 2 subsets, with 2 elements it has 4, and with 3 elements it has 8, so a set with n elements has 2^n subsets. Each element is either in or out of a subset, which explains the doubling. The empty set appears in every list.
Mathematical conclusion

An element belongs to a set; a subset is a set whose every element belongs to another set. Every set has 2^n subsets, including the empty set and the set itself.

Chapter 8 · Mathematical development

8.1 Sets, elements and subsets

Big idea

Define a set clearly, list each element once and distinguish “element of” from “subset of”.

A set is a well-defined collection. x ∈\in∈ A means x is an element of A; B ⊆\subseteq⊆ A means every element of B is also in A. Order and repeated listings do not change a set.

The empty set ∅\emptyset∅ has no elements and is a subset of every set. A set with n distinct elements has 2ⁿ subsets, because each element is either included or excluded.

Worked example · Subsets of {a,b,c}

Choose included or excluded for each element.

  1. 2×2×2 = 8 subsets.
  2. ∅\emptyset∅, {a}, {b}, {c}, {a,b}, {a,c}, {b,c}, {a,b,c}.
8 subsets.

Watch for this misconception

∈\in∈ relates an element to a set; ⊆\subseteq⊆ relates one set to another. {a} ⊆\subseteq⊆ {a,b}, but a ∈\in∈ {a,b}.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 8 · Sets and classification
Chapter 8 · Investigation · before 8.2

Investigate · Fill the overlap first

Your task

In a group of 30 students, 18 play football, 14 play music and 7 do both. Complete the Venn diagram counts.

RegionCountCalculation
Both football and music
Football only
Music only
Neither
Total

What do you notice?

  • Why is the overlap placed first, before the “only” regions?
  • How many students are in at least one club, and how did you avoid double counting?
Observation. The overlap of 7 is counted in both totals, so it must be placed first: football only is 18 − 7 = 11 and music only is 14 − 7 = 7. At least one club is 11 + 7 + 7 = 25, so 5 students are in neither.
Mathematical conclusion

Place the overlap first, then the “only” regions, then the outside region. The union counts every element once, which is why the overlap is subtracted.

Chapter 8 · Mathematical development

8.2 Venn diagrams and set operations

Big idea

Place the overlap first, then the “only” regions, then the outside region.

Union A ∪\cup∪ B contains elements in A or B or both. Intersection A ∩\cap∩ B contains elements in both. Complement A′\prime′ contains elements in the universal set ξ\xiξ that are not in A.

For finite sets, n(A∪\cup∪B)=n(A)+n(B)−n(A∩\cap∩B). Subtract the overlap once because it was counted in both totals.

Worked example · Complete a Venn diagram

ξ\xiξ has 30 students; 17 help at a fair, 14 at a concert, 6 at both.

  1. Both: 6. Fair only: 17−6=11. Concert only: 14−6=8.
  2. At least one: 11+6+8=25. Neither: 30−25=5.
Regions 11, 6, 8, 5.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 8 · Sets and classification
Chapter 8 · Investigation · before 8.3

Investigate · Classify by properties

Your task

Place each number in the correct region of the number-set diagram: −3, 0, 0.75, 1/3, −2.5, √2.

NumberWhole?Integer?Rational?Irrational?
−3
0
0.75
1/3
√2

What do you notice?

  • Which numbers belong to more than one set, and what does that show?
  • Why is √2 not rational, even though it is written with a symbol?
Observation. Whole numbers sit inside integers, integers sit inside rational numbers, and irrational numbers such as √2 sit outside them. A number can belong to several sets at once: −3 is an integer and a rational number, and 0.75 and 1/3 are both rational.
Mathematical conclusion

Classify a number by the properties it has, not by the way it is written. Rational numbers are exactly those that can be written as a fraction of two integers.

Chapter 8 · Mathematical development

8.3 Number sets and the real line

Big idea

Classify a number by the sets it belongs to, not by the way it is written.

Natural numbers N\mathbb{N}N are counting numbers (here 1,2,3,…); whole numbers add 0; integers Z\mathbb{Z}Z add negatives; rationals Q\mathbb{Q}Q are ratios of integers with nonzero denominator. Real numbers R\mathbb{R}R include rationals and irrationals.

Thus natural numbers are a subset of whole numbers, which are a subset of integers, which are a subset of rationals, which are a subset of reals. A terminating or repeating decimal is rational. Non-repeating, non-terminating decimals such as √2 and π are irrational.

Worked example · Classify −3, 0, 0.75 and √2

Use the most specific familiar set, then note wider membership.

  1. −3 is an integer and rational.
  2. 0 is whole, integer and rational.
  3. 0.75 = 3/4 is rational.
  4. √2 is irrational and real.
All four are real; only √2 is irrational.
Chapter 8 · Practice · Criterion A

Criterion A practice · 8.3 Number sets and the real line

Watch for this misconception

A number can belong to several sets. “Rational” does not mean “fraction-looking”; 0.5 and 1/2 are both rational.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 8 · Sets and classification
Chapter 8 · Investigation · before 8.4

Investigate · Define before you count

Your task

A sports centre has 80 members (simulated data). 46 use the pool, 37 use the gym and 19 use both. Answer the questions below.

QuestionRegion neededAnswer
How many use the pool or the gym?
How many use exactly one facility?
How many use neither?
What percentage of members use both?

What do you notice?

  • Why must the universal set be stated before any count?
  • What percentage of the 80 members use at least one facility?
Observation. With 80 members in the universal set: pool only is 46 − 19 = 27 and gym only is 37 − 19 = 18, so 64 use at least one facility and 16 use neither. Exactly one facility is 27 + 18 = 45, and 19 of 80 is 23.75%.
Mathematical conclusion

Define the universal set and the categories before counting, and state whether “or” includes the overlap. Every percentage needs its denominator.

Chapter 8 · Mathematical development

8.4 Sets in surveys and decisions

Big idea

Define the universal set and categories before counting; state whether “or” includes overlap.

A survey count is only meaningful with its universal set. “Pool users” may include people who also use the gym; “pool only” excludes them.

Use a Venn diagram or table to organise counts, check that regions sum to the total, and translate the result into a decision with a stated assumption.

Worked example · A centre audit

80 members: 44 pool, 37 gym, 18 both.

  1. Pool only 26; gym only 19; both 18; neither 17.
  2. At least one: 63, which is 78.75% of 80.
Regions 26, 18, 19, 17; 78.75% use at least one.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measure · MYP Year 1 · Chapter 09

Perimeter, area, surface area and volume

Choosing the right measure—length, area, surface area or volume—connects geometric structure to material use, capacity and cost.

Inquiry questions
  • Factual: Which formulas give the perimeter, area, surface area and volume of common shapes, and what units does each use?
  • Conceptual: Why does a triangle have half the area of a parallelogram with the same base and height, and why is a prism's volume a cross-section times a length?
  • Debatable: When is an estimate more useful than an exact measurement, and how much rounding is sensible when buying materials?
Second editionGlobalization and sustainability
Chapter 9 · Opener

Perimeter, area, surface area and volume

Choosing the right measure—length, area, surface area or volume—connects geometric structure to material use, capacity and cost.

Engagement

How can a community project estimate turf, paving, fencing, soil and paint without confusing boundary, surface and space?

Learning goals

  • Distinguish perimeter, area, surface area and volume.
  • Calculate with triangles, quadrilaterals, circles and composites.
  • Use nets and prism formulas with correct units.
  • Convert capacity, compare packaging and evaluate a project budget.

Related concepts: Measurement, Space

Global context: Globalization and sustainability

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 9 · Perimeter, area, surface area and volume
Chapter 9 · Investigation · before 9.1

Investigate · Boundary or surface?

Your task

For a 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle, find the perimeter and the area. Then cut it along a diagonal and find the perimeter and area of each triangle.

ShapePerimeter (cm)Area (cm²)Units used
Rectangle 6 × 4
Each triangle from the diagonal
Parallelogram, base 6, height 4
Triangle, base 6, height 4

What do you notice?

  • What happens to the perimeter when the rectangle is cut, and what happens to the total area?
  • Why does the triangle have half the area of the parallelogram with the same base and height?
Observation. The rectangle has perimeter 20 cm and area 24 cm². Cutting along a diagonal keeps the total area at 24 cm² but increases the total perimeter, because the cut edge is new boundary. A triangle on base 6 and height 4 has area 12 cm², half of the parallelogram.
Mathematical conclusion

Perimeter adds lengths in ordinary units; area multiplies two dimensions in square units. Choose the quantity the task needs before calculating.

Chapter 9 · Mathematical development

9.1 Perimeter and area of triangles and quadrilaterals

Big idea

Choose the quantity the task needs: boundary length, covered surface or space inside.

Perimeter is the total boundary length. Area measures surface in square units. Rectangle area = length×width; triangle area = ½×base×perpendicular height; parallelogram area = base×height.

A trapezoid with parallel sides a and b and perpendicular height h has area ½(a+b)h. The height must be perpendicular to the parallel sides, not a slant edge.

Worked example · A triangle and a trapezoid

Triangle: base 8 cm, height 5 cm. Trapezoid: parallel sides 6 and 10 cm, height 4 cm.

  1. Triangle: ½×8×5 = 20 cm².
  2. Trapezoid: ½×(6+10)×4 = 32 cm².
20 cm² and 32 cm².
Chapter 9 · Practice · Criterion A

Criterion A practice · 9.1 Perimeter and area of triangles and quadrilaterals

Watch for this misconception

Do not use a slant side as the height. Do not report area in cm or perimeter in cm².

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 9 · Perimeter, area, surface area and volume
Chapter 9 · Investigation · before 9.2

Investigate · Around and inside a circle

Your task

Measure the diameter and circumference of three circular objects, then divide the circumference by the diameter.

ObjectDiameter d (cm)Circumference C (cm)C ÷ d
Class average

What do you notice?

  • What value does C ÷ d approach, and what is it called?
  • If the radius is 3 cm, find the circumference and the area using π ≈ 3.14.
Observation. Every object gives C ÷ d close to 3.14, so C = πd = 2πr. For r = 3 cm, C ≈ 18.84 cm and A = πr² ≈ 28.26 cm².
Mathematical conclusion

The ratio of circumference to diameter is constant for every circle. Use C = πd and A = πr², and label results as approximate when π is rounded.

Chapter 9 · Mathematical development

9.2 Circles and composite shapes

Big idea

Identify radius and diameter, then split a composite shape into familiar pieces.

For a circle, diameter d=2r. Circumference C=πd=2πr; area A=πr². In this chapter use π≈3.14 unless told otherwise, and label results as approximate.

A semicircle has half the circle area and a curved boundary of πr. For a composite plan, add areas of non-overlapping pieces and trace only the outer boundary for fencing.

Worked example · A semicircular stage

Diameter 12 m, so radius 6 m.

  1. Area = ½×3.14×6² = 56.52 m².
  2. Curved boundary = 3.14×6 = 18.84 m.
Area ≈56.52 m²; arc ≈18.84 m.
Chapter 9 · Practice · Criterion A

Criterion A practice · 9.2 Circles and composite shapes

Watch for this misconception

The diameter is not part of the outer boundary when the semicircle is attached to a rectangle along that edge.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 9 · Perimeter, area, surface area and volume
Chapter 9 · Investigation · before 9.3

Investigate · Nets and surface area

Your task

Sketch a net for a cuboid measuring 3 cm by 2 cm by 4 cm, then find its surface area. Repeat for the same cuboid with the top face removed.

SolidFacesFace areas (cm²)Surface area (cm²)
Closed cuboid
Open-topped cuboid
Cube of side 3 cm

What do you notice?

  • How many faces does each solid have, and which face is missing in the open-topped version?
  • Why is surface area not the same as volume?
Observation. A closed cuboid has six faces in three matching pairs: 2(3×2) + 2(3×4) + 2(2×4) = 12 + 24 + 16 = 52 cm². Removing the top face (12 cm²) leaves 40 cm². A cube of side 3 cm has surface area 6 × 9 = 54 cm².
Mathematical conclusion

A net shows every outside face; surface area adds the face areas, not the space inside. Identify which faces are actually exposed before adding.

Chapter 9 · Mathematical development

9.3 Nets and surface area

Big idea

A net shows every outside face; surface area adds face areas, not the space inside.

A net is a flat pattern that folds into a solid. The surface area of a closed cuboid is 2(lw+lh+wh). For an open-topped box, omit the top face.

Use square units for surface area. Painting an outside surface depends on area; filling the box depends on volume. Keep the two quantities separate.

Worked example · An open-topped raised bed

Length 1.2 m, width 0.6 m, height 0.5 m.

  1. Base: 1.2×0.6 = 0.72 m².
  2. Two long sides: 2×1.2×0.5 = 1.20 m². Two short sides: 2×0.6×0.5 = 0.60 m².
Outside area = 2.52 m².
Chapter 9 · Practice · Criterion A

Criterion A practice · 9.3 Nets and surface area

Watch for this misconception

A closed cuboid has six faces; an open-topped bed has five. Do not paint an imaginary top.

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 9 · Perimeter, area, surface area and volume
Chapter 9 · Investigation · before 9.4

Investigate · Volume and capacity

Your task

Fill a 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm box with 1 cm cubes. Count the cubes, then work out how many 1 L bottles fill a 1 m³ tank.

QuantityCalculationResultUnits
Cubes in the box
Volume of the box
Litres in 1 m³
Litres in 1 cm³

What do you notice?

  • How does the number of cubes relate to the formula V = l × w × h?
  • Why is 1 m³ equal to 1,000 L and not 100 L?
Observation. The box holds 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cubes, so its volume is 24 cm³. A 1 m cube is 100 cm on each side, so it holds 100 × 100 × 100 = 1,000,000 cm³, and since 1 cm³ = 1 mL, that is 1,000 L.
Mathematical conclusion

Volume measures space in cubic units and capacity measures how much a container holds. Lengths scale by 100, areas by 10,000 and volumes by 1,000,000 between metres and centimetres.

Chapter 9 · Mathematical development

9.4 Prisms, volume and capacity

Big idea

Volume measures space; capacity measures how much a container can hold.

A prism has a constant cross-section. Volume = cross-section area × length. For a cuboid, V=lwh; for a triangular prism, V=(½×base×height)×length.

Capacity conversions: 1 cm³ = 1 mL; 1,000 cm³ = 1 L; 1 m³ = 1,000 L. Convert units before multiplying or dividing.

Worked example · A tank and a prism

Tank 50 cm × 30 cm × 40 cm; triangular prism with cross-section base 8 cm, height 5 cm, length 14 cm.

  1. Tank volume 60,000 cm³ = 60 L.
  2. Prism volume ½×8×5×14 = 280 cm³.
60 L; 280 cm³.
Chapter 9 · Practice · Criterion A

Part IV · Shape, structure and measureChapter 9 · Perimeter, area, surface area and volume
Chapter 9 · Action and projects

Project connections

Mathematics becomes service and action when it answers a need that other people have. Each connection below is student-led: choose one, plan it with your teacher and follow your school’s requirements and supervision.

Service as Action

Community need
A school garden has no reliable way to order soil, mulch or paint, so materials are over-ordered.
Mathematical connection
Perimeter, area, surface area and volume (sections 9.1–9.4).
Proposed action
Measure the beds, compute the soil volume and paint area, and produce an ordering sheet the gardener can reuse each term.
Expected impact
The garden orders the right quantities, reducing waste and cost.
Student reflection
Record how you checked the measurements, how much allowance you made for error, and what you would measure differently.

Community Project connection

Project idea
A water-harvesting estimate for a community building.
Community need
Roof catchment volume is often guessed, so tanks are sized badly.
Research question
How much rain can a given roof area collect in a season, and what tank size does that imply?
Mathematics
Area, volume, capacity and unit conversion.
Action and outcome
Measure a roof, model the collected volume for a stated rainfall and recommend a tank size.
Beneficiaries
Community building users and maintenance staff.
Evidence
Measurements, volume model, tank recommendation and the assumptions stated.

Personal Project connection · MYP 5

Personal interest
Architecture, product design or gardening.
Learning goal
To design an object or space whose measurements are calculated rather than guessed.
Product or outcome
A scaled design with an ordering list for materials.
Mathematics
Perimeter, area, surface area, volume and unit conversion.
Process
Measure or specify dimensions, compute each quantity, cost the materials and evaluate the design.
Evidence
Product, process journal and an evaluation against the stated learning goal. This is an MYP 5-oriented extension: follow your school's Personal Project requirements and supervision.

Service as Action is not the same as completing an exercise: it requires action that benefits others and a reflection on that action. The Community Project connection suits the MYP community project completed by students finishing MYP in Year 3 or Year 4, and the Personal Project connection is an adaptable MYP 5-oriented extension. They are deliberately different from one another.

Part V · Data and decisions · MYP Year 1 · Chapter 10

Data, tables and graphs

Data displays and summaries make patterns visible, but choices of grouping, scale and denominator shape the claims that seem reasonable.

Inquiry questions
  • Factual: What is a variable, and which display suits categorical, discrete and continuous data?
  • Conceptual: Why can two graphs of the same data support different claims, and how do averages summarise a distribution?
  • Debatable: When is a statistic fair to publish, and when does the choice of display do the arguing?
Second editionFairness and development
Chapter 10 · Opener

Data, tables and graphs

Data displays and summaries make patterns visible, but choices of grouping, scale and denominator shape the claims that seem reasonable.

Engagement

How can the same survey support a fair decision without letting a misleading graph or an unstated denominator do the arguing?

Learning goals

  • Classify variables and organise frequency or two-way tables.
  • Construct and interpret bar and pie charts.
  • Summarise distributions with dot plots, histograms and averages.
  • Describe trends and detect misleading scales or claims.

MYP lens

Key concept: Relationships

Related concepts: Representation, Pattern

Global context: Fairness and development

ATL focus. In order for a student to process and communicate information, students must organise data, choose an appropriate representation, calculate summaries and justify a claim with its limitations.

Language bank: variable · categorical · nominal · ordinal · discrete · continuous · frequency · two-way table · bar chart · pie chart · sector angle · dot plot · histogram · mean · median · mode · range · outlier · trend

Part V · Data and decisionsChapter 10 · Data, tables and graphs
Chapter 10 · Investigation · before 10.1

Investigate · What kind of variable?

Your task

Classify each item as categorical (nominal or ordinal) or numerical (discrete or continuous), and state the unit where there is one.

ItemCategorical or numericalSub-typeUnit
Lunch choice
Number of siblings
Height
Shirt size code
Rating from 1 to 5

What do you notice?

  • Which items are numbers used only as labels?
  • Why does the type of variable decide which average makes sense?
Observation. Lunch choice is nominal, a 1 to 5 rating is ordinal, the number of siblings is discrete numerical, height is continuous numerical, and a shirt size code is categorical even though it uses digits. Averages only make sense for numerical variables.
Mathematical conclusion

Identify what was measured, the unit, the population and the type of variable before summarising anything.

Chapter 10 · Mathematical development

10.1 Data, variables and tables

Big idea

Identify what was measured, the unit, the population and the type of variable before summarising.

Data are recorded values. A categorical variable names groups (nominal) or ordered categories (ordinal). A numerical variable is discrete if it counts separate values, or continuous if it measures on a scale.

A frequency table lists categories or intervals and their counts. Frequencies must sum to the number of observations. A two-way table shows how two categories overlap.

Worked example · Classify variables

Lunch choice, year group, number of siblings and height.

  1. Lunch choice: nominal categorical.
  2. Year group: ordinal categorical (or discrete numerical code).
  3. Siblings: discrete numerical. Height: continuous numerical.
The variable type guides the display and summary.

Part V · Data and decisionsChapter 10 · Data, tables and graphs
Chapter 10 · Investigation · before 10.2

Investigate · Choosing a display

Your task

Display the lunch survey as a bar chart and as a pie chart: school 96, packed 74, off-site 30, out of 200 students (simulated data).

DisplayWhat it shows bestSector angle or bar heightLimitation
Bar chart
Pie chart
Check: sector angle for school

What do you notice?

  • How do you compute the sector angle for “school”?
  • Which display would you use to compare year groups, and why?
Observation. School is 96/200 = 48% of the total, so its sector angle is 0.48 × 360° = 172.8°. Bars compare categories directly; a pie shows parts of one whole but is poor for many similar categories or several groups side by side.
Mathematical conclusion

Use bars to compare categories and sectors to show parts of one whole. Label axes, start the frequency axis at zero and state the denominator.

Chapter 10 · Mathematical development

10.2 Bar charts and pie charts

Big idea

Use bars to compare categories and sectors to show parts of one whole.

A bar chart uses equal-width bars with heights proportional to frequency. Label axes, start the frequency axis at zero and keep spacing consistent.

A pie chart represents a whole by 360°. Sector angle = category frequency/total × 360°. Percentages should sum to 100% apart from stated rounding.

Worked example · Lunch choices for 200 students

School 96, packed 74, off-site 30.

  1. School: 96/200×360 = 172.8°.
  2. Packed: 74/200×360 = 133.2°.
  3. Off-site: 30/200×360 = 54°.
Angles sum to 360°.

Criterion A practice · 10.2 Bar charts and pie charts

Watch for this misconception

A pie chart is poor for comparing many similar categories or several groups side by side; a clustered bar chart is clearer.

Part V · Data and decisionsChapter 10 · Data, tables and graphs
Chapter 10 · Investigation · before 10.3

Investigate · Centre and spread

Your task

For the values 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 20, find the mean, median, mode and range. Then remove the 20 and recompute.

SummaryWith 20Without 20Change
Mean
Median
Mode
Range

What do you notice?

  • Which summary changed most when the 20 was removed, and why?
  • Which average best describes the remaining seven values, and for what question?
Observation. With the 20 the mean is 64 ÷ 8 = 8 and the median is 6.5; without it the mean is 44 ÷ 7 ≈ 6.29 and the median is 6. The mean moved much more than the median because the 20 pulls it upwards.
Mathematical conclusion

Describe shape, centre and spread together. An outlier moves the mean a lot and the median very little, so choose the average that fits the data and the question.

Chapter 10 · Mathematical development

10.3 Dot plots, histograms and averages

Big idea

Describe shape, centre and spread; choose an average that fits the data and the question.

A dot plot shows individual values. A histogram groups continuous or finely measured numerical data into intervals; with equal widths, bar height is frequency. State the boundary rule.

Mean = sum÷count; median is the middle ordered value (or mean of the two middle values); mode is most frequent; range = maximum−minimum. Outliers pull the mean more than the median.

Worked example · Summarise 30 screen-time values

The ordered data have sum 4,740; the 15th and 16th values are 135 and 140; 120 occurs four times.

  1. Mean = 4740/30 = 158 min.
  2. Median = (135+140)/2 = 137.5 min.
  3. Mode = 120 min; range = 360−45 = 315 min.
Mean 158; median 137.5; mode 120; range 315 minutes.

Part V · Data and decisionsChapter 10 · Data, tables and graphs
Chapter 10 · Investigation · before 10.4

Investigate · Read the scale

Your task

Two graphs show the same five values: 88, 72, 80, 90, 96 (simulated data). One starts its axis at 0 and one at 70. Describe what each graph suggests.

GraphAxis startVisual impressionIs it misleading?
Graph A0
Graph B70
Same data, table—

What do you notice?

  • What claim does each graph support, and which claim is better supported by the data?
  • What three things should you check before accepting a visual claim?
Observation. Graph B makes a small rise from 88 to 96 look dramatic because the axis starts at 70; Graph A shows the change in proportion. The data themselves show a rise of 8 over five years, which is a modest change on a scale of 0 to 100.
Mathematical conclusion

Read the scale, the denominator and the time order before accepting a visual claim. A truncated axis can make a small change look large without any number being wrong.

Chapter 10 · Mathematical development

10.4 Trends, comparisons and misleading graphs

Big idea

Read the scale, denominator and time order before accepting a visual claim.

A line graph or time-ordered bar chart can show change over time. Describe direction, size of change and exceptions; do not call every fluctuation a trend.

Misleading displays include truncated axes, unequal intervals, 3-D distortion, area used for a one-dimensional value, missing denominators and selective time windows. Compare like with like.

Worked example · Test “sales doubled”

Sales rose from 50 to 90.

  1. Increase = 40.
  2. Percentage increase = 40/50×100 = 80%.
The claim is false: sales rose by 80%, not 100%.

Check your progress

Work through the checklist without looking back. Anything you cannot do yet is a target for the mixed practice.

I can now

  • I can classify variables and organise data in frequency or two-way tables.
  • I can construct and interpret bar charts, pie charts, dot plots and histograms.
  • I can summarise a distribution with an appropriate average and describe its spread.
  • I can describe a trend and detect a misleading scale or an unstated denominator.

Reflect

Part V · Data and decisionsChapter 10 · Data, tables and graphs
Chapter 10 · Action and projects

Project connections

Mathematics becomes service and action when it answers a need that other people have. Each connection below is student-led: choose one, plan it with your teacher and follow your school’s requirements and supervision.

Service as Action

Community need
School notices publish percentages without denominators, so families cannot judge them.
Mathematical connection
Data displays, averages and misleading graphs (sections 10.1–10.4).
Proposed action
Audit 10 school notices, classify each figure as supported or unsupported, and present a short guide to the school office.
Expected impact
Notices state their denominators, so readers can judge the figures.
Student reflection
Record the figures you found, how you checked each one and what the office changed.

Community Project connection

Project idea
A community data display on a topic chosen with local residents.
Community need
Local decisions are argued with anecdote rather than evidence.
Research question
What can a small, well-designed survey show about a local question, and what can it not show?
Mathematics
Variables, tables, displays, averages and claims.
Action and outcome
Design and run a survey of 30 to 50 respondents, publish a display with stated denominators and limitations.
Beneficiaries
Community members, local leaders and students.
Evidence
Survey questions, data table, display and a report that states the limitations.

Personal Project connection · MYP 5

Personal interest
Journalism, public information or sport analysis.
Learning goal
To evaluate statistical claims in public reporting.
Product or outcome
A short evaluation of three published claims using data you collect or verify.
Mathematics
Averages, displays, percentage change and misleading scales.
Process
Select claims, collect or verify data, recompute the summaries and write the evaluation.
Evidence
Product, process journal and an evaluation against the stated learning goal. This is an MYP 5-oriented extension: follow your school's Personal Project requirements and supervision.

Service as Action is not the same as completing an exercise: it requires action that benefits others and a reflection on that action. The Community Project connection suits the MYP community project completed by students finishing MYP in Year 3 or Year 4, and the Personal Project connection is an adaptable MYP 5-oriented extension. They are deliberately different from one another.
